How this curriculum works:
Read this one first. It is the only lesson that is about the curriculum rather than about Greek.

**The stages are an ordered route and nothing more.** No dates, no pacing, no gates. Do them in order, move on when something is solid, repeat a lesson as often as you like. Eleven stages, and stage 11 does not end — *ad astra*.

**Every lesson teaches its point in full and then tells you what to practise.** You should never have to open a source to learn the thing the lesson is about. The sources listed on a lesson are there if you want it said again, in another voice, or with more drills.

**Any term is explained where it is first used.** If a grammar word turns up unexplained — case, aspect, clitic, declension — that is a fault in the lesson.

**The levels are the Ellinomatheia levels**, A1 to C2, as published by the Centre for the Greek Language. **No exam is taken.** They are used because they are an honest description of what "knowing some Greek" means, and because the free graded material and past papers are built against them.

**Two tracks run alongside the stages**, drawn as their own row of cards beneath the stage deck. They are not later projects:

| Track | Run it from | What it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Spelling** | stage 2 onward | the orthography, drilled. Which *i* a word takes, the accent rules, final *-ν*, punctuation, handwriting joins. |
| **Forms** | stage 3 onward | the declension and conjugation tables, as reference and as drills — nouns, adjectives, pronouns, verbs, aspect pairs, irregulars. |

**The rate: one track lesson for every three or four route lessons**, alternating between the two once both are open. They are short, and the Spelling ones are drills rather than reading.

**Why spelling gets a track of its own.** Modern Greek has five vowel sounds and about a dozen ways of writing them: *ι η υ ει οι υι* all say *i*. Which spelling a word takes is a fact about that word, inherited from Ancient Greek, and there is no rule that predicts it. It is the main memory burden in the language and it is the one thing here that genuinely rewards drilling.

**Four habits run underneath everything:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Read aloud** | every example in every lesson, out loud, at speaking speed. Greek is not a language to learn silently. |
| **The deck** | the gold card above the stage list. Nouns with their gender, verbs as aspect pairs, spelling cards, phrases. Ten new a day. |
| **Pimsleur** | half an hour, most days, through stages 1 to 4. It is for the mouth, not the grammar. |
| **Input** | graded listening and reading from this stage onward, native material from stage 8 |

**What this curriculum is not for** is the next lesson, and it is worth reading before anything else: the language of the liturgy is not this language.

**Practice.** Read the next lesson, then start the alphabet. Begin Pimsleur lesson 1 today — it needs nothing you have not got.
What this curriculum is for, and what it:
You said why: the liturgy, and the Greek people at church. Those are two different languages and the honest version of this curriculum starts by saying so.

**The people at church speak Modern Greek**, and that is what this teaches: the language of conversation, of the hall after the service, of the family that invites you to eat, of what they read and watch and argue about. By the end of the route you will be able to hold your end of that.

**The liturgy is not in Modern Greek.** It is in several older registers at once:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Gospel and Epistle readings** | Koine Greek, first century — the Greek of the New Testament |
| **The Old Testament readings** | the Septuagint, older still, and translated out of Hebrew |
| **The hymnography and the prayers** | Byzantine liturgical Greek, deliberately archaic even when it was written |
| **The service books** | the same, with a learned grammar that Modern Greek has dropped |

**What a fluent Modern Greek speaker actually gets from the Liturgy**: a good deal of the vocabulary, the shape of most sentences, the sense of a passage, and a running sense of familiarity. What they miss: the verb forms, the participles doing the structural work, the datives, the optatives, and whole clauses whose grammar modern Greek no longer has. Greeks in the pews are in that position too — the Liturgy is understood by habit and repetition as much as by grammar.

**So it is a separate curriculum, by your ruling** — classical Greek, moving into theological and liturgical Greek. That is where the Koine verb system, the participles, the hymn texts, the service books and the katharevousa register belong, and it will be built as its own route.

**What this one gives you towards it, which is a lot:**

- **The alphabet and the sound system**, which are shared.
- **Several thousand words**, most of which are the same words, often with the ancient meaning still visible behind the modern one.
- **The case system**, reduced in the modern language but recognisably the same machinery.
- **The habit of reading Greek** rather than decoding it.

**And the church vocabulary of the modern language is in this route**, because that is the language of the parish rather than of the altar: the feasts and the fasts, the names, the greetings on a feast day, the social and family words, what people call the priest and what they call each other.

**The one thing to keep straight.** When you are at church and something is incomprehensible, the question is which language it was in. If it was the chanter, it was not your Greek failing. If it was the man next to you, it was.

**Practice.** None. Start the alphabet.
The alphabet: twenty-four letters:
The whole writing system, in one lesson, before the detail. Twenty-four letters, each with a capital and a small form, and almost all of them say one sound.

| | | Name | Sounds like |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Α | α | άλφα | *a* in *father* |
| Β | β | βήτα | *v* |
| Γ | γ | γάμα | no English equivalent — a soft *gh* |
| Δ | δ | δέλτα | *th* in *this* |
| Ε | ε | έψιλον | *e* in *bet* |
| Ζ | ζ | ζήτα | *z* |
| Η | η | ήτα | *ee* |
| Θ | θ | θήτα | *th* in *think* |
| Ι | ι | γιώτα | *ee* |
| Κ | κ | κάπα | *k* |
| Λ | λ | λάμδα | *l* |
| Μ | μ | μι | *m* |
| Ν | ν | νι | *n* |
| Ξ | ξ | ξι | *ks* |
| Ο | ο | όμικρον | *o* in *lot* |
| Π | π | πι | *p* |
| Ρ | ρ | ρο | a tapped *r* |
| Σ | σ / ς | σίγμα | *s* |
| Τ | τ | ταυ | *t* |
| Υ | υ | ύψιλον | *ee* |
| Φ | φ | φι | *f* |
| Χ | χ | χι | no English equivalent — as in Scottish *loch* |
| Ψ | ψ | ψι | *ps* |
| Ω | ω | ωμέγα | *o* in *lot* |

**Three facts that make this much easier than it looks:**

1. **Greek is spelled consistently in one direction.** Given the spelling you can always say the word correctly. Going the other way — hearing a word and knowing how to write it — is the hard direction, and that is what the Spelling track is for.
2. **Seven letters are the same as English in shape and sound**: Α Ε Ι Κ Ο Τ and Μ, roughly.
3. **Five are false friends** — they look English and are not: **Β** is *v*, **Η** is *ee*, **Ρ** is *r*, **Υ** is *ee*, **Χ** is a throaty *h*. Those five cause nearly every beginner misreading.

**Three letters say two sounds at once**: Ξ is *ks*, Ψ is *ps*, and Ζ is a plain *z*.

**Three different letters say *ee***: Η, Ι and Υ. Two say *o*: Ο and Ω. This is not redundancy to be tidied away — it is the spelling carrying the word's history, and it is why Greek spelling has to be learned word by word.

**Sigma has two small forms**: σ everywhere, and **ς** at the end of a word. Same letter, same sound.

**The next six lessons take the letters four at a time**, with their sounds, their handwriting and words you can already read. Do not try to memorise this table — it is here to look at once, and to come back to.

**Practice.** Read the twenty-four names out loud, down the column. Then find Greek text — a package in a shop, a Wikipedia article, anything — and read ten letters off it by name without worrying about the words.
Α α, Β β, Γ γ, Δ δ:
The first four, with the two that trip up every English speaker.

**Α α — *álfa*.** The sound *a* in *father*, always, in every position. Greek vowels never change with stress and never glide.

- **αν** — if · **αλλά** — but · **άλλα** — other things

**Β β — *víta*.** The sound is **v**, not *b*. This is the first false friend and it never relents: *Βασίλης* is *Vasílis*, *βιβλίο* is *vivlío*.

- **βιβλίο** — book · **βάζο** — vase · **αβγό** — egg

**Where did *b* go?** It is written **μπ**, and it has its own lesson. Ancient Greek's beta softened to *v* and the gap was filled by a two-letter spelling.

**Γ γ — *gáma*.** The hardest sound in the alphabet for an English speaker, because English has nothing like it. It is the voiced version of the *ch* in Scottish *loch*: the back of the tongue comes near the soft palate, but does not touch, and the voice keeps going.

- **γάλα** — milk · **γάτα** — cat · **μεγάλος** — big

**How to find it.** Say *ga* and then relax the back of the tongue until the stop becomes a hum. Or say a Spanish *agua*, or a Dutch *g*. A plain English *g* is wrong but intelligible; aim for the softer sound and let it arrive over weeks.

**Before *e* and *i* it changes completely** — to a *y* sound, as in *yes*. That has its own lesson.

**Δ δ — *délta*.** The sound is **th** in *this*, *that*, *mother* — voiced. Not *d*.

- **δάσκαλος** — teacher · **δέκα** — ten · **δρόμος** — road, street

**Where did *d* go?** It is written **ντ**, and it also has its own lesson.

**Writing them.** α is written as one stroke, like a handwritten *a* with no tail. β is a tall loop with two bellies, descending below the line. γ looks like a *y* and sits below the line. δ is a loop with a tail curling left over the top.

**Practice.** Read aloud, five times each: **γάλα, γάτα, βιβλίο, δέκα, δάσκαλος, αλλά**. Then write each letter ten times, saying its sound as you write. Then find three words in any Greek text that contain γ and read them aloud.
Ε ε, Ζ ζ, Η η, Θ θ:
Four more, including the second of the *ee* letters and the voiceless *th*.

**Ε ε — *épsilon*.** The sound *e* in *bet*. Short, clear, never a glide.

- **ένα** — one · **εγώ** — I · **έχω** — I have

**Ζ ζ — *zíta*.** A plain **z**, as in *zoo*. In Greek it is a single sound, never *dz* — that is **τζ**, later.

- **ζωή** — life · **ζάχαρη** — sugar · **μαζί** — together

**Η η — *íta*.** The sound **ee**. Identical in sound to Ι and Υ, and different in spelling because the word's history says so.

- **η** — the (feminine) · **ήλιος** — sun · **μήνας** — month

**That is now two letters saying *ee*** — Η and Ι — and a third is coming. The sound is the same; which letter a word uses is part of the word.

**Θ θ — *thíta*.** The sound **th** in *think*, *thanks* — voiceless, the pair of δ.

- **θέλω** — I want · **θάλασσα** — sea · **Θεός** — God

**δ and θ together** give Greek both English *th* sounds as separate letters, which English spelling never managed. Say *this* and *think* and notice your voice is on for one and off for the other: that is δ against θ.

**Writing them.** ε is a small backwards 3 or a looped *e*. ζ descends below the line with a tail. η looks like an *n* with a long right leg below the line. θ is a circle with a bar through the middle — in handwriting, often a loop and a crossing stroke.

**Three words to notice**, because you already know them in English: **θέατρο** (theatre), **ζώο** (animal — as in *zoo*), **ηλεκτρικός** (electric). English took thousands of words from Greek, and from here on you will keep recognising them — that is a real advantage and it accelerates.

**Practice.** Read aloud five times each: **θέλω, θάλασσα, ζωή, ήλιος, έχω, εγώ**. Then write each of the four letters ten times. Then say *this–think, δ–θ* ten times, checking your voice goes on and off.
Ι ι, Κ κ, Λ λ, Μ μ:
Four easy ones, and the third letter that says *ee*.

**Ι ι — *ghióta*.** The sound **ee**. The third and last single letter for that sound.

- **είναι** — is, are · **ίδιος** — same · **πίνω** — I drink

**Κ κ — *kápa*.** A plain **k**, with no puff of air after it. English *k* in *kit* comes with a breath; Greek κ does not. The difference is small and it is one of the things that makes an accent.

- **καλά** — well, fine · **κάνω** — I do, I make · **καφές** — coffee

**Before *e* and *i* it softens** to something between *k* and the *c* in *cute*. It happens automatically if you are relaxed; nothing needs to be done about it deliberately.

**Λ λ — *lámda*.** An **l** as in *let* — always the light, front *l*, never the dark *l* of English *ball* or *milk*.

- **λέω** — I say · **καλός** — good · **πόλη** — city

**Μ μ — *mi*.** A plain **m**.

- **μέρα** — day · **μαμά** — mum · **μικρός** — small

**Four letters, and you can now read a great deal.** Try these, which use only letters from the first three lessons: **καλά, μικρός, μεγάλος, γάλα, μέρα, θέλω, μαζί, κάνω**.

**Writing them.** ι is a single stroke with no dot — Greek never dots the iota. κ is written like a small English *k* with a soft join. λ is a tall stroke leaning left with a leg to the right, not the English *l*. μ descends below the line, like a *u* with a tail on the left.

**The μ trap.** Handwritten μ is easy to mistake for *u*, and handwritten ν — coming next — looks like English *v*. Those two confusions are the commonest reading errors in handwritten Greek.

**Practice.** Read aloud five times each: **καλημέρα** (good morning — now fully readable), **καλά, μικρός, μέρα, πόλη, καφές**. Then write ι κ λ μ ten times each. Then write *καλημέρα* out five times by hand, saying it as you write.
Ν ν, Ξ ξ, Ο ο, Π π:
Four more, including one letter that carries two consonants.

**Ν ν — *ni*.** A plain **n**. The lower-case form looks like an English *v*, which is the second of the handwriting traps.

- **ναι** — yes · **νερό** — water · **άνθρωπος** — person, human being

**Ξ ξ — *ksi*.** The two sounds **ks** in one letter, as in English *fox* or *axe*. It exists because Greek had a lot of *ks* and gave it a letter.

- **ξέρω** — I know · **ξένος** — foreigner, stranger · **έξι** — six

**Ο ο — *ómikron*.** The sound *o* in *lot* — short, round, with no glide. Its name means "small o", which tells you Ω was once the long one; in the modern language they sound identical.

- **όχι** — no · **όνομα** — name · **καλό** — good

**Π π — *pi*.** A plain **p**, again with no puff of air.

- **πόλη** — city · **πατέρας** — father · **παιδί** — child

**Now you can read whole phrases.** **Καλημέρα** — good morning. **Ναι** and **όχι** — yes and no. **Πώς σε λένε;** is coming shortly and you can already read most of it.

**Writing them.** ν is a single *v*-shaped stroke. ξ descends below the line with two loops and a tail — the hardest letter to write and worth practising on its own. ο is a plain circle. π is two downstrokes with a bar across the top, and in handwriting is often written as a single wavy stroke.

**A word about άνθρωπος.** It is *ánthropos*, and it is in English inside *anthropology* and *philanthropy*. This is the pattern worth noticing early: most Greek words with abstract meaning are already in English somewhere, usually in a learned word, and the connection is a free vocabulary multiplier.

**Practice.** Read aloud five times each: **ναι, όχι, νερό, όνομα, παιδί, έξι, ξέρω**. Then write ν ξ ο π ten times each, with ξ twenty. Then read these out: **άνθρωπος, πατέρας, πόλη, καλό**.
Ρ ρ, Σ σ ς, Τ τ, Υ υ:
Four more, with the two-formed sigma and the third false friend.

**Ρ ρ — *ro*.** The sound is a **single tapped r** — the tongue flicks once against the ridge behind the teeth. It is the *r* of Spanish *pero* or Italian *caro*, not the English *r* and not a rolled Scottish *r* either.

- **ρολόι** — clock, watch · **ώρα** — hour · **καρδιά** — heart

**English *r* is the giveaway.** An English *r* in Greek is immediately audible as foreign, more than almost any other substitution. The tap is learnable: say *very* quickly, American-style, and notice the tongue touching — that touch, done deliberately and once, is ρ.

**Σ σ ς — *síghma*.** The sound **s**. Two lower-case forms:

- **σ** everywhere inside or at the start of a word
- **ς** only at the end of a word

Same letter, same sound, and the final form is not optional — *δάσκαλος* ends in ς and never σ.

- **σήμερα** — today · **σπίτι** — house · **κόσμος** — world

**Before a voiced consonant it becomes *z*** — *κόσμος* is heard as *kózmos*, *Ισραήλ* as *Izraíl*. It happens by itself.

**Τ τ — *taf*.** A plain **t**, no puff of air, and the tongue touches further forward than in English.

- **τι** — what · **τώρα** — now · **τρία** — three

**Υ υ — *ípsilon*.** The sound **ee** — the third letter and the last of them. On its own it is not common in modern words, but it is everywhere in **digraphs**, which are the next few lessons: **ου, αυ, ευ, υι**.

- **ύστερα** — afterwards · **ύψος** — height · **μύτη** — nose

**So: Η, Ι, Υ all say *ee*.** Add the pairs **ει** and **οι** and there are five ways to write that one sound. This is the central fact of Greek spelling and the reason the Spelling track exists.

**Writing them.** ρ is a circle with a straight tail descending — not a *p*. σ is a circle with a flat lead-in at the top. ς is a small hook descending below the line. τ is a downstroke with a bar. υ is like an English *u*, which is a third handwriting trap: handwritten υ and υ-looking ν need care.

**Practice.** Read aloud five times each: **σήμερα, σπίτι, τώρα, ώρα, καρδιά, κόσμος**. Then the tap: say **ρολόι, ώρα, τρία** ten times, with one flick of the tongue each time. Then write ρ σ ς τ υ ten times each, and write **δάσκαλος** five times, checking the final ς.
Φ φ, Χ χ, Ψ ψ, Ω ω:
The last four letters, including the one sound English speakers find hardest after γ.

**Φ φ — *fi*.** A plain **f**. It is written with one letter where English uses *ph* — and English only uses *ph* in words it took from Greek.

- **φίλος** — friend · **φως** — light · **καφές** — coffee

**Χ χ — *khi*.** The sound of *ch* in Scottish *loch* or German *Bach* — the back of the tongue near the soft palate, voiceless, with air hissing through. Not *k*, not English *ch*, not *h*.

- **χαίρω** — I am glad · **χέρι** — hand · **όχι** — no · **χρόνος** — time, year

**Before *e* and *i* it softens** to something like the *h* in a strongly whispered *huge*. So **χέρι** and **όχι** have a lighter sound than **χρόνος** and **χαρά**. This happens by itself if you let it.

**How to find χ.** Start from γ, which you met three lessons ago, and switch the voice off. Or say *k* and let the stop leak instead of releasing cleanly.

**Ψ ψ — *psi*.** The two sounds **ps** in one letter, as in English *lapse* — and at the start of a word too, which English never does: **ψάρι** is *psári*, both sounds pronounced.

- **ψάρι** — fish · **ψωμί** — bread · **ψυχή** — soul

**Ω ω — *oméga*.** The sound *o* in *lot* — identical to Ο. Its name means "big o" and in Ancient Greek it was the long one; the modern language dropped the length and kept both letters.

- **ώρα** — hour · **ψωμί** — bread · **εγώ** — I

**So now the full set of overlaps:** three letters say *ee* (η ι υ), two say *o* (ο ω), and the digraphs add more of both. Nothing else in the alphabet overlaps.

**Writing them.** φ is a tall loop descending below the line with a vertical stroke through it. χ is an *x* written with a longer descending stroke. ψ is a *y* with a bowl at the top — like a trident. ω is a *w* with rounded humps, written in one stroke.

**You can now read every letter in Greek.** Try these, which use the whole alphabet between them: **ψωμί, ψάρι, φίλος, χέρι, όχι, χρόνος, ώρα, φως, ψυχή, εγώ**.

**Practice.** Read aloud five times each: **χέρι, χρόνος, όχι, ψωμί, ψάρι, φίλος**. Then the χ drill: say **χα, χε, χι, χο, χου** ten times and notice how the sound lightens before ε and ι. Then write φ χ ψ ω ten times each.
The two sigmas, and the shapes that catc:
A short practical lesson: the letter with two forms, and the half-dozen shapes that cause nearly every misreading.

**Sigma, again, because it matters.** σ inside and at the start of a word, **ς** at the end, and nowhere else. The rule has no exceptions in modern printing:

- **σπίτι** · **κόσμος** · **Σάββατο** · **δάσκαλος** · **σήμερα**

**In all capitals there is only Σ** — ΔΑΣΚΑΛΟΣ, not ΔΑΣΚΑΛΟς.

**The lunate sigma** — ϲ, a plain crescent used for both positions — turns up in church inscriptions, icons and old books. Same letter. Worth recognising for exactly the place where you will see it.

**The shapes that catch English readers**, and this list is worth keeping:

| You see | It is not | It is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **ν** | English *v* | *n* |
| **υ** | English *u* | *ee* |
| **ρ** | English *p* | *r* |
| **β** | English *b* | *v* |
| **η** | English *n* | *ee* |
| **γ** | English *y* | the soft *gh* |
| **χ** | English *x* | the *loch* sound |
| **ξ** | — | *ks* |
| **ω** | English *w* | *o* |
| **μ** | English *u* | *m* |

**The pairs that look alike within Greek:**

- **ν** and **υ** — the first is pointed, the second rounded. In handwriting this is a real difficulty and context usually decides it.
- **ζ** and **ξ** — both descend with a tail; ξ has two loops above.
- **θ** and **φ** — both are tall loops; θ has a crossbar in the bowl, φ a full vertical stroke through it.
- **σ** and **ο** — in fast handwriting, σ is a circle with a lead-in flick at the top.

**Capitals are easier**, because most of them are familiar from maths and from English: Α Β Γ Δ Ε Ζ Η Θ Ι Κ Λ Μ Ν Ξ Ο Π Ρ Σ Τ Υ Φ Χ Ψ Ω. Only Γ, Δ, Θ, Λ, Ξ, Π, Σ, Φ, Ψ and Ω are shapes English does not have, and all ten are recognisable from mathematics.

**Where you will read capitals most**: shop signs, church inscriptions, icon labels, headlines, and anything monumental. Icons in particular are almost always capitals, abbreviated, with no accents: **ΙΣ ΧΣ** for Ἰησοῦς Χριστός, **ΜΡ ΘΥ** for Μήτηρ Θεοῦ. Noticing that now will make a church interior legible long before the Liturgy is.

**Practice.** Read aloud, slowly: **ΚΑΛΗΜΕΡΑ, ΕΞΟΔΟΣ, ΤΡΑΠΕΖΑ, ΦΑΡΜΑΚΕΙΟ, ΑΡΤΟΠΟΙΕΙΟ**. Those are *good morning, exit, bank, pharmacy, bakery*, and all five are signs you would see in a Greek street. Then write out **κόσμος, δάσκαλος, Σάββατο** by hand, checking each sigma.
The five vowel sounds, and the many ways:
The central fact about Greek spelling, stated once, plainly, before the digraph lessons.

**Modern Greek has five vowel sounds.** That is all: *a, e, i, o, u*. No long and short, no reduced vowels, no diphthongs in the English sense, and no change under stress. Every vowel in every word is one of those five, pronounced the same every time.

**And it has about a dozen ways of writing them:**

| Sound | Written as | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **a** | α | **άλλος**, **γάλα** |
| **e** | ε, αι | **ένα**, **παιδί** |
| **i** | ι, η, υ, ει, οι, υι | **πίνω**, **ήλιος**, **μύτη**, **είναι**, **σπίτι** (οι in **σπίτια**), **υιός** |
| **o** | ο, ω | **όχι**, **ώρα** |
| **u** | ου | **μου**, **ούτε** |

**So the reading direction is easy and the writing direction is hard.** See a word and you can say it. Hear a word and the spelling is a question with five or six possible answers — and the answer is a historical fact about that particular word.

**Why it is like this.** In Ancient Greek those spellings were different sounds: η was a long *e*, υ was a French *u*, ει and οι were real diphthongs. The sounds merged over two thousand years and the spelling did not follow. Modern Greek spelling is therefore a record of ancient pronunciation, which is also why it connects so directly to the older language.

**What follows for you, practically:**

1. **Reading is never the problem.** From here you can pronounce any Greek word you see, correctly, including words you have never met.
2. **Spelling has to be learned per word**, and that is what the Spelling track and the deck are for. A spelling card asks "which *i* does this word take" and there is no shortcut.
3. **The endings are the high-leverage part.** Word endings recur constantly and their spellings are fixed by grammar rather than by history: *-ει* in a verb, *-η* in a feminine noun, *-οι* in a masculine plural. Learning those patterns settles most of the spelling of most words. That is the first thing the Spelling track does.

**One early and useful rule.** The ending *-ει* on a verb (**γράφει** — he writes) and the ending *-η* on a feminine noun (**πόλη** — city) are the two commonest *i* endings, and they are decided by grammar, not memory.

**Practice.** Say these aloud and notice that the sound is identical in all of them: **πίνω, ήλιος, μύτη, είναι, οικία**. Then write them from dictation — read them, cover them, write them — and see how many spellings you got right. That gap is what the track closes.
The vowel digraphs: αι ει οι ου υι:
Two letters, one sound, five pairs. These are not diphthongs — nothing glides — and they are extremely common.

| Digraph | Sound | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **αι** | *e*, as in ε | **παιδί** (child) · **και** (and) · **είναι** (is) |
| **ει** | *i* | **είμαι** (I am) · **πείνα** (hunger) · **γράφει** (he writes) |
| **οι** | *i* | **οικογένεια** (family) · **οι** (the, masc. plural) · **ποιος** (who) |
| **ου** | *u* | **μου** (my, of me) · **πού** (where) · **λουλούδι** (flower) |
| **υι** | *i* | **υιός** (son) — rare, and mostly in formal or church language |

**και is the commonest word in Greek** and it is a digraph: *ke*. Hearing it as *kai* is the single most frequent beginner error in reading aloud.

**ου is the only way to write the *u* sound.** There is no single letter for it — the ancient letter υ that once said *u* drifted to *i* and left the digraph behind.

**How to tell a digraph from two separate vowels.** Sometimes the two letters really are two sounds in two syllables, and Greek marks that in two ways:

1. **A diaeresis** — two dots — on the second letter: **παϊδάκια** (lamb chops) is *pa-i-dákia*, not *pe-dákia*. **Μάιος** (May) is *Má-i-os*.
2. **The accent on the first letter**: **άι**, **όι** and so on are read as two syllables. **Κάιρο** (Cairo).

**Without one of those marks, the pair is a digraph** and says one sound. That is a reliable rule in both directions, and it is why the diaeresis is not decorative.

**The accent on a digraph goes on the second letter**: **παίζω** (I play), **είμαι** (I am), **πού** (where), **μποϊκοτάζ**. The pair is one vowel, so it takes one accent, on the second half.

**Where the digraphs matter most: the endings.** They are not scattered randomly through the language — they cluster in grammatical endings, which is good news:

- **-ει** ends a third-person singular verb: **γράφει**, **θέλει**, **έχει**
- **-ουν** ends a third-person plural: **γράφουν**, **θέλουν**
- **-οι** ends a masculine plural noun: **δάσκαλοι**, **φίλοι**
- **-αι** ends a handful of common words: **και**, **είναι**, **ναι**

**Practice.** Read aloud five times each: **και, είμαι, είναι, παιδί, μου, πού, οικογένεια**. Then say **και** twenty times as *ke* until *kai* stops feeling available. Then write from dictation: **παιδί, είναι, λουλούδι, φίλοι**.
αυ and ευ — where the υ turns into a con:
The two digraphs that behave differently from the rest, because the second letter becomes a consonant.

**αυ and ευ are not vowel pairs.** The υ becomes **f** or **v**, depending on what follows:

| | Before a voiceless consonant | Before a vowel or a voiced consonant |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **αυ** | *af* — **αυτός** (he, this) | *av* — **αύριο** (tomorrow) |
| **ευ** | *ef* — **ευχαριστώ** (thank you) | *ev* — **Εύα**, **ευάγγελο** |

**The voiceless consonants are κ π τ φ θ χ σ ξ ψ.** Before any of those, υ is *f*. Before everything else — vowels, and β γ δ ζ λ μ ν ρ — it is *v*.

**The two words you will use every day:**

- **αυτός / αυτή / αυτό** — he / she / it, and this. Said *aftós, aftí, aftó*.
- **ευχαριστώ** — thank you. Said *efharistó*, with the χ before the ι lightened.

**Why this happens.** In Ancient Greek these were genuine diphthongs — *au*, *eu*. The second half hardened into a consonant and the spelling stayed, which is the same story as every other mismatch in Greek orthography.

**ηυ exists and is vanishingly rare** — **ηύρα** and a few verb forms. Treat it as *if* / *iv* and move on.

**Where you meet these constantly:**

- **ευ-** begins a large family of words meaning *well* or *good*: **ευχαριστώ** (thank you), **ευτυχία** (happiness), **ευκολία** (ease), **Ευαγγέλιο** (Gospel — literally *good news*), **ευλογία** (blessing).
- **αυτ-** begins the self words: **αυτός**, **αυτοκίνητο** (car — *self-moving*), **αυτόματος**.

**The church connection is immediate here.** **Ευαγγέλιο**, **ευλογία**, **ευχαριστία** (thanksgiving — and the word behind *Eucharist*) all start with this digraph, and all are Modern Greek words as well as liturgical ones. You will hear them in the hall as well as in the service.

**Practice.** Read aloud ten times: **ευχαριστώ** — and get *ef-ha-ri-stó* rather than *ev-* or *eu-*. Then: **αυτός, αυτή, αυτό, αύριο, ευτυχία, Ευαγγέλιο**. Then sort these by whether the υ is *f* or *v*: **αυτοκίνητο, εύκολο, αύριο, ευχή, ευλογία**.
The consonant digraphs: μπ ντ γκ γγ:
Where Greek keeps the sounds *b*, *d* and *g* — which the single letters β, δ and γ stopped making two thousand years ago.

| Written | Sound at the start of a word | Sound inside a word |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **μπ** | *b* — **μπαίνω** (I enter) | *mb* — **αμπέλι** (vineyard) |
| **ντ** | *d* — **ντομάτα** (tomato) | *nd* — **πέντε** (five) |
| **γκ** | *g* — **γκαράζ** (garage) | *ng* — **αγκαλιά** (embrace) |
| **γγ** | — never initial | *ng* — **αγγελία** (announcement), **άγγελος** (angel) |

**So Greek has no letter *b*, *d* or *g* and writes them with pairs.** The pairs are genuinely single sounds at the start of a word; inside a word, many speakers keep a light nasal before the stop, and many do not. Both are standard, and it varies by region and by speaker. Do whichever is comfortable.

**γγ and γκ sound the same inside a word.** Which one a word takes is spelling, not sound: **άγγελος** has γγ, **αγκαλιά** has γκ.

**Where they come from.** Mostly two places: loanwords, which need the sounds Greek lost (**μπάνιο** bath, **ντους** shower, **γκολ** goal, **μπύρα** beer), and old compounds where a nasal met a stop (**πέντε**, **άνδρας**).

**The nasal before a stop happens across words too**, and this is worth knowing early because it makes fast speech hard to parse. The final **-ν** of a small set of words — **τον, την, δεν, μην, σαν** — assimilates to the next word's first consonant:

- **τον πατέρα** is heard as *tom-batéra*
- **την Κυριακή** is heard as *tin-gyriakí*
- **δεν ξέρω** is heard as *den-gzéro*

**Nothing is written differently** — the sound just changes. The Spelling track takes final *-ν* properly, because when to write it is a real question.

**The church word to notice: άγγελος.** Angel, written with γγ, said *ánghelos*, and the same word in the Liturgy, in the hymns, and on every icon of the Archangels — **ΑΡΧΑΓΓΕΛΟΣ ΜΙΧΑΗΛ**.

**Practice.** Read aloud five times each: **μπαίνω, μπύρα, ντομάτα, πέντε, άγγελος, αγκαλιά, γκολ**. Then say **τον πατέρα, την Κυριακή, δεν πειράζει** at speaking speed, letting the nasal do what it wants. Then write from dictation: **πέντε, ντομάτα, άγγελος**.
τσ and τζ:
Two more consonant pairs, both single sounds, both common — and one of them is the sound English writes *ts*.

**τσ — the *ts* sound**, as in English *cats* or Italian *pizza*. Voiceless.

- **τσάι** — tea · **κορίτσι** — girl · **παπούτσια** — shoes · **τσίπουρο** — the spirit

**τζ — the voiced version**, as in English *adze*, or close to the *j* in *jam* for most speakers.

- **τζάκι** — fireplace · **τζατζίκι** — tzatziki · **Τζον** — John, written in Greek

**Both are single sounds**, not two. **τσάι** is two syllables — *tsá-i* — with the diaeresis-free αι split by the accent, and the τσ is one consonant at the front.

**Where they come from.** Overwhelmingly from Turkish, Italian and Slavic borrowings, which is why they cluster in food, household and everyday words — exactly the vocabulary you will meet first. Ancient Greek had neither sound.

**τσ is also how Greek writes foreign *ch* and *ts***: **τσεκ** (cheque), **τσιπ** (chip), **πίτσα** (pizza).

**A note on Cypriot, which is stage 10.** Cypriot Greek has sounds the standard language does not, including a genuine *sh* and *ch* — so **τσ** in a Cypriot word is often heard as English *ch*, and the dialect also keeps double consonants as real geminates. If you have heard Cypriots speak and thought it sounded quite different, that is largely this and it is not an accident of accent.

**The whole consonant inventory is now in place**, which means you have met every sound in the language. From here the alphabet lessons are about the accent, the hand and the eye.

**Practice.** Read aloud five times each: **τσάι, κορίτσι, παπούτσια, τζάκι, τζατζίκι**. Then say **κορίτσι** and **κοριτσάκι** (little girl), which is the diminutive pattern you will meet constantly. Then write out **παπούτσια** and **τζατζίκι** by hand.
γ before ε and ι, and the γι sound:
The letter that changes its sound depending on what follows it — and it is one of the commonest letters in the language.

**γ has two sounds:**

| Before | Sound | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **α ο ου** and consonants | the soft *gh* from the alphabet lesson | **γάλα**, **γόνατο**, **γουρούνι**, **γράφω** |
| **ε αι ι η υ ει οι** | a *y* sound, as in English *yes* | **γέρος** (old man), **γεια** (hi), **γίνομαι** (I become), **γυρίζω** (I turn) |

**So γεια σου** — the everyday hello — is *yá-su*, not *ghia-su*. **γυναίκα** (woman) is *yinéka*. **γεια** and **γυναίκα** are two of the first fifty words you will use, so this is not a detail.

**The same thing happens to χ and κ**, less dramatically: before *e* and *i* both soften towards the front of the mouth. **χέρι** is lighter than **χαρά**; **και** is lighter than **κάνω**. You do not have to do anything about it — the tongue does it on its own if you are relaxed — but noticing it explains why the same letter seems to sound different in different words.

**γι before another vowel is one sound**, a *y* glide: **γιατί** (why, because) is *ya-tí*, **γιαγιά** (grandmother) is *ya-yá*, **γιος** (son) is *yos*.

**And that is why ι is sometimes a consonant.** In **παιδιά** (children), **θειος** (uncle), **καρδιά** (heart), the ι glides into the next vowel rather than standing as its own syllable. It is the same *y* sound; Greek simply writes it with ι.

**ευλογία, θεολογία, λειτουργία** — the *-ία* ending in these is two syllables, *-í-a*, because the accent is on the ι. Compare **καρδιά**, where the accent is on the α and the ι glides. The accent tells you which it is, every time, which is one more reason the accent is compulsory.

**γγ and γκ keep the hard sound**, as the digraph lesson said — **άγγελος** is *ánghelos* and not *ányelos* — because the γ there is part of a pair.

**Practice.** Read aloud five times each: **γεια σου, γυναίκα, γιατί, γιαγιά, γέρος, γάλα, γράφω**. Then alternate: **γάλα – γεια, γόνατο – γέρος, γράφω – γυρίζω** ten times, hearing the two sounds switch. Then say **παιδιά, καρδιά, λειτουργία** and notice which ι glides and which stands alone.
The stress accent: what it marks, and wh:
One mark, one job, and it is not optional — Greek is one of the few languages that writes its stress on every word.

**What it marks.** Which syllable is stressed. **Nothing else** — no length, no pitch, no vowel quality. It is a single mark: **ά έ ή ί ό ύ ώ**.

**Every word of two syllables or more carries one**, and exactly one: **καλημέρα, άνθρωπος, ευχαριστώ, σπίτι, παιδί**.

**Monosyllables do not**, with a handful of exceptions kept to prevent confusion:

| Accented | Unaccented | The difference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **πού** (where?) | **που** (that, who) | question against relative |
| **πώς** (how?) | **πως** (that) | the same |
| **ή** (or) | **η** (the, feminine) | the only accented monosyllable most people notice |

**Why it is compulsory: Greek has hundreds of pairs that differ only in stress.** This is the fact that makes the accent load-bearing rather than decorative:

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **πότε** — when? | **ποτέ** — never |
| **πάρα** (as in παρά) | **παρά** — but, except |
| **γέρος** — old man | **γερός** — strong, healthy |
| **νόμος** — law | **νομός** — prefecture |
| **μόνος** — alone | **μονός** — single, odd-numbered |

**Reading a word with the stress in the wrong place makes it a different word, or no word.** It is also the most immediately audible mistake a learner makes — more than any consonant.

**So the accent is part of the spelling, always.** A word written without it is misspelled, and a word learned without it is half-learned. Every card in the deck carries it.

**Capitals are the exception.** A word in all capitals takes no accents — **ΚΑΛΗΜΕΡΑ**, **ΕΞΟΔΟΣ** — and a single initial capital keeps its accent only if the accent is on that letter: **Άννα**, **Έλληνας**. Shop signs and icon inscriptions therefore give you no help with stress, which is worth knowing when you try to read them aloud.

**The old system.** Before 1982 Greek was written polytonically: three accents, two breathings, and a lot of rules. The modern language uses one accent and no breathings — the **monotonic** system. You will see the old system in church books, in older editions and in anything deliberately traditional, which is another reason the later classical curriculum exists.

**Practice.** Read aloud, in pairs, ten times: **πότε – ποτέ**, **γέρος – γερός**, **μόνος – μονός**. Then read these with the stress exactly where it is written: **ευχαριστώ, καλημέρα, άνθρωπος, οικογένεια, ελληνικά**. Then write five words you know, from memory, with their accents.
Where the stress falls: the last three s:
The rules that govern where the accent can be, which matter because the accent moves when a word changes form.

**The rule of limitation: the stress is always on one of the last three syllables.** Never the fourth from the end, in any word, ever. Greek has no word stressed further back than that.

**The three positions have names**, and they are worth knowing because grammar books use them:

| Position | Name | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Last syllable | *λήγουσα* | **καλό**, **παιδί**, **αυτός** |
| Second from last | *παραλήγουσα* | **σπίτι**, **μέρα**, **θέλω** |
| Third from last | *προπαραλήγουσα* | **άνθρωπος**, **δάσκαλος**, **θάλασσα** |

**Why it moves.** When a word gains a syllable — in the genitive, in the plural, with an attached pronoun — the stress may have to move forward to stay within the last three:

- **άνθρωπος** → **ανθρώπου** (of the person). The word gained nothing, but the ending changed and the stress moved forward one.
- **δάσκαλος** → **δασκάλου** · **θάλασσα** → **θαλάσσης** (formal genitive)
- **το μάθημα** → **του μαθήματος**

**That movement is a rule, not a quirk**, and the Forms track sets it out with the declensions. For now the thing to notice is that the accent is part of the ending pattern rather than fixed to the word.

**The second accent.** When a weak pronoun attaches to a word stressed on the third-from-last syllable, Greek writes **two** accents:

- **ο δάσκαλος** + **μου** → **ο δάσκαλός μου** (my teacher)
- **το όνομα** + **μου** → **το όνομά μου** (my name)
- **δώσε** + **μου το** → **δώσε μού το** (give it to me)

**Why.** The pronoun counts as a syllable of the phrase, so the original stress is now fourth from the end, which is not allowed — so a second stress is added within the limit. It looks strange and it is entirely regular.

**Where a digraph is involved, the accent goes on the second letter**: **παίζω**, **είμαι**, **πούλησα**. And a diaeresis plus an accent can both appear: **Μαΐου** (of May).

**The practical consequence for speaking.** Greek rhythm is stress-timed, like English, but the stress is *where the mark says* and not where instinct puts it. English speakers tend to stress Greek words on the second-from-last syllable by default, which is right about half the time.

**Practice.** Read these aloud, exaggerating the marked syllable: **άνθρωπος, ανθρώπου, δάσκαλος, δασκάλου, θάλασσα, το όνομά μου, ο φίλος μου**. Then take five words from the deck and say where each is stressed by name — λήγουσα, παραλήγουσα or προπαραλήγουσα.
Reading your first sentences aloud:
Everything so far, used. These are real sentences, every one of them useful, and you can read all of them already.

**Greetings and the first exchange:**

| Greek | Said | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Καλημέρα! | *kalimé-ra* | Good morning |
| Καλησπέρα! | *kalispé-ra* | Good evening |
| Γεια σου. | *yá su* | Hi (to one person) |
| Γεια σας. | *yá sas* | Hello (polite, or to several) |
| Τι κάνεις; | *ti káni-s* | How are you? |
| Καλά, ευχαριστώ. | *kalá, efharistó* | Fine, thanks |
| Εσύ; | *esí* | And you? |
| Πώς σε λένε; | *pos se léne* | What is your name? |
| Με λένε… | *me léne* | My name is… |
| Χάρηκα. | *hárika* | Pleased to meet you |

**Note the question mark.** That **;** is the Greek question mark, not a semicolon. Its own lesson is coming.

**Three sentences to read carefully**, because each one contains something from the last few lessons:

**1. Καλημέρα, τι κάνεις;** — the η in καλημέρα says *i*; the αι in κάνεις is *e*.

**2. Ευχαριστώ πολύ.** — thank you very much. The ευ is *ef*, and the ώ at the end is stressed.

**3. Αυτός είναι ο φίλος μου.** — he is my friend. αυ is *af*; ει in είναι is *i*; the αι in είναι is *e*.

**Read them out loud, slowly, then at speed.** Then read them again listening for your own ρ — one tap — and your own γ in *γεια*, which should be a *y*.

**The politeness fork, which matters at church.** **Γεια σου** and **τι κάνεις** are singular and familiar; **γεια σας** and **τι κάνετε** are plural and polite. With someone older than you, someone you have just met, and the priest, use the plural. With a friend, the singular. Getting this wrong is the most common social error a learner makes, and Greeks are forgiving about it — but it is worth getting right from the first week.

**What to do with these this week.** Say them to yourself, out loud, every day. Say them in the car. Say **καλημέρα** on Sunday to someone who will say it back. The whole point of putting them in stage 1 is that they work before you know any grammar at all.

**Practice.** Read the table aloud five times, top to bottom. Then say the three sentences from memory. Then write **Με λένε** + your name, by hand, in Greek letters.
Handwriting: the lowercase letters:
Writing Greek by hand, which you asked for and which is worth the fortnight it takes. It also fixes the letters in a way reading never does.

**Why handwriting and not just typing.** Writing a letter by hand makes you decide its shape, which makes you notice the differences between ν and υ, ζ and ξ, θ and φ. It also means you can write a name, a note, a shopping list or a date — and that you can read other people's handwriting, which is a separate skill and genuinely hard.

**The letters that sit on the line**, like English *a*: α ε ι κ ν ο π σ τ υ ω — ten of them, all simple.

**The letters that descend below the line**: β γ ζ η θ μ ξ ρ ς φ χ ψ. Twelve, and more than English has. A line of Greek handwriting therefore looks busier below the baseline.

**The ones with a real shape to learn:**

| Letter | How it is written |
| --- | --- |
| **α** | one stroke, like a handwritten *a* with no ascender |
| **β** | a tall loop from the top, down below the line, with two bellies |
| **γ** | like a *y*: down-right, then the tail below the line |
| **δ** | a loop anticlockwise with the tail curling up and left over the top |
| **ζ** | a flat top, down to the left, tail below the line |
| **θ** | an oval with a crossbar inside it |
| **λ** | a tall stroke leaning left, then a leg to the right — not an English *l* |
| **μ** | starts below the line on the left, up and over like a *u* with a tail |
| **ξ** | two small loops stacked, then a tail below the line. The hardest one. |
| **π** | often one wavy stroke: down, across, down |
| **ρ** | a circle with a straight tail descending — not a *p*, whose tail is the stroke |
| **σ** | a circle with a small lead-in flick at the top |
| **ς** | a hook that drops below the line, used only at the end of a word |
| **φ** | a tall oval with a vertical stroke through it, descending |
| **ψ** | a bowl with a vertical stroke through it, descending |
| **ω** | one stroke, two rounded humps, like a *w* with no corners |

**Do not join everything.** Greek handwriting is semi-joined: letters are often written separately or in small groups, and no one joins ρ or ς to what follows. Copying printed shapes slowly and separately is the right way to start.

**Write the accent as you write the word**, not afterwards. It is part of the word.

**What to practise on.** Your own name, the greetings from the last lesson, and the words from the deck. Copying is fine; copying out loud is better.

**Practice.** Write the alphabet in lower case, three times, saying each letter's name as you write it. Then write out the ten greetings from the last lesson by hand. Then write **ξ**, **ζ**, **ψ** ten times each, because those three are the ones that will stay ugly longest.
Handwriting: the capitals, and when Gree:
The capitals are easier than the lowercase, and the rules for using them are not the English ones.

**All twenty-four:** Α Β Γ Δ Ε Ζ Η Θ Ι Κ Λ Μ Ν Ξ Ο Π Ρ Σ Τ Υ Φ Χ Ψ Ω.

**Fourteen are identical in shape to a Latin capital** — Α Β Ε Ζ Η Ι Κ Μ Ν Ο Ρ Τ Υ Χ — though four of those say something different: Β is *v*, Η is *i*, Ρ is *r*, Χ is the *loch* sound.

**Ten have their own shapes**, and every one of them is familiar from mathematics: Γ Δ Θ Λ Ξ Π Σ Φ Ψ Ω.

**Writing them is straightforward**: they are geometric, they sit on the line, and none descends. Σ is three strokes, Ξ is three horizontals, Ψ is a vertical with a bowl, Ω is a circle open at the bottom with two feet.

**When Greek capitalises**, which is less than English:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The first word of a sentence** | as in English |
| **Proper names** | people, places, countries: **Ελλάδα**, **Αθήνα**, **Γιώργος** |
| **Feast days and months?** | months are **lower case** — **Ιανουάριος** is capitalised as a name but days of the week and months are commonly written lower case in running text; both are seen |
| **Nationalities** | the noun is capitalised — **Έλληνας**, **Άγγλος** — but the adjective is not: **ελληνικά** (Greek, the language), **αγγλικά** |
| **Titles** | only the first word, usually |

**And what it does not capitalise:** the pronoun *I* (**εγώ**, lower case), days of the week in most styles, months in most running text, and adjectives of nationality.

**Accents on capitals.** A single initial capital keeps its accent if the stress is on it — **Άννα**, **Έλληνας**, **Όλγα** — and **all-capital text takes no accents at all**: **ΑΘΗΝΑ**, **ΕΞΟΔΟΣ**, **ΚΑΛΗΜΕΡΑ**.

**Which is why signs and inscriptions are hard to read aloud.** A shop sign gives you the letters and not the stress. **ΦΑΡΜΑΚΕΙΟ** is *farmakío*, and nothing on the sign tells you so.

**Church inscriptions are the extreme case**: all capitals, no accents, and heavily abbreviated. The standard ones are worth learning now because they are everywhere:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **ΙΣ ΧΣ** | Ἰησοῦς Χριστός — Jesus Christ |
| **ΜΡ ΘΥ** | Μήτηρ Θεοῦ — Mother of God |
| **ΙΧΘΥΣ** | fish — the acrostic |
| **Ο ΩΝ** | "the One who is", in Christ's halo |
| **ΝΙΚΑ** | conquers — as in ΙΣ ΧΣ ΝΙΚΑ |

**Practice.** Write the capitals three times each. Then write your own name and three Greek names in capitals. Then read these aloud and put the stress in the right place from memory: **ΑΘΗΝΑ, ΘΕΣΣΑΛΟΝΙΚΗ, ΕΛΛΑΔΑ, ΚΥΡΙΑΚΗ, ΦΑΡΜΑΚΕΙΟ**.
Typing Greek:
Getting Greek out of a keyboard, on Linux, with accents — a ten-minute setup that you will use for the rest of this curriculum.

**The layout.** Greek keyboards map onto QWERTY almost phonetically, which means you can type Greek by touch almost immediately:

| Key | Letter | Key | Letter |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| a | α | n | ν |
| b | β | o | ο |
| g | γ | p | π |
| d | δ | r | ρ |
| e | ε | s | σ |
| z | ζ | t | τ |
| h | η | y | υ |
| u | θ | f | φ |
| i | ι | x | χ |
| k | κ | c | ψ |
| l | λ | v | ω |
| m | μ | j | ξ |
| w | ς | q | : |

**The ones to memorise** are the five that are not phonetic: **u** gives θ, **c** gives ψ, **v** gives ω, **j** gives ξ, **w** gives final ς.

**The accent is a dead key.** Press **;** (the semicolon key) and then the vowel: **;** + **a** gives **ά**. For a diaeresis, use **shift-;** then the vowel — **ϊ**. For both at once, there is a dedicated combination, and on most layouts **;** then **shift-i** gives **ΐ**.

**On Omarchy / Hyprland**, add the layout to your input config and set a toggle:

```
input {
    kb_layout = us,gr
    kb_options = grp:alt_shift_toggle
}
```

Then **Alt+Shift** switches between English and Greek. Check it with `hyprctl getoption input:kb_layout` if it does not take.

**The alternative: Greeklish.** Typing Greek in Latin letters — *kalimera, ti kaneis* — which Greeks do constantly in messages. It is real and you will see it, and it is worth being able to read. Do not write the curriculum's exercises in it: writing in Greek letters is half of why you are learning them.

**Where you will type Greek:** the deck's answers, the writing exercises from stage 2 onward, searching the Triantafyllidis dictionary, and messaging anyone.

**Searching dictionaries without accents works** — the Portal for the Greek Language and most tools ignore them — so you can look a word up before you know where its stress goes.

**Practice.** Set the layout up now. Type the ten greetings from the earlier lesson, with their accents. Then type your own name in Greek letters. Then type **ευχαριστώ πολύ** and check the ώ is accented rather than plain.
Double consonants, and what they do not:
A short lesson with a useful negative in it: Greek writes double consonants and does not pronounce them double.

**The doubles that occur:** λλ, μμ, νν, ρρ, σσ, ττ, ππ, κκ, and the special cases γγ and γκ from the digraph lesson.

**In Standard Modern Greek they are single sounds:**

| Written | Said |
| --- | --- |
| **αλλά** (but) | *alá* |
| **θάλασσα** (sea) | *thálasa* |
| **γράμμα** (letter) | *ghráma* |
| **Σάββατο** (Saturday) | *sávato* |
| **εννιά** (nine) | *eniá* |

**So the doubling is purely orthographic** — a fossil of Ancient Greek, where the consonant really was held longer. It is one more thing the Spelling track has to drill, because nothing in the sound tells you that **θάλασσα** has two σ and **πόλη** has one λ.

**The two exceptions that are not exceptions:** γγ and γκ, which represent a nasal plus a stop and really are two sounds — **άγγελος**, **αγκαλιά**.

**And μμ, νν across a word boundary** keep a double length naturally in careful speech: **τον νόμο** (*ton nómo*) has an audible double *n* because it spans two words.

**Cypriot is different and this is the clearest single marker of it.** Cypriot Greek **does** pronounce geminates: *θάλασσα* comes out with a held *ss*, and the dialect has double consonants in places the standard language does not. If you have heard Cypriot Greek and found it percussive compared with Athenian, that is largely this. Stage 10 takes it properly.

**Why it matters now rather than later.** Three reasons: you will not hear the doubles, so you cannot write them from dictation and must learn them; the spelling is a reliable fingerprint of a word's ancient form, which helps when the later Greek curriculum starts; and the Cypriot difference is a real one you will hear at church if there are Cypriots in the parish.

**Practice.** Read aloud, with single consonants: **αλλά, θάλασσα, γράμμα, Σάββατο, εννιά, άλλος**. Then write them from dictation — read, cover, write — and check which doubles you missed. Then say **τον νόμο** and hear the double that is real.
The sounds Greek has, and the ones it ha:
A sorting lesson for the accent: what your mouth has to learn, and what it has to stop doing.

**Greek sounds that English does not have, and all four are in common words:**

| Sound | Letter | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| soft voiced *gh* | **γ** before α ο ου | **γάλα**, **γουρούνι** |
| the *loch* sound | **χ** before α ο ου | **χρόνος**, **χαρά** |
| the single tapped *r* | **ρ** | **ώρα**, **τρία** |
| unaspirated stops | **κ π τ** | **κάνω**, **πόλη**, **τώρα** |

**The unaspirated stops are the subtle one.** English *p*, *t* and *k* come with a puff of air at the start of a word — hold a hand in front of your mouth and say *pot* and you will feel it. Greek π, τ, κ have no puff. It is a small difference that accounts for a surprising amount of what makes a foreign accent in Greek.

**English sounds that Greek does not have, and using them is the commonest giveaway:**

| English sound | What Greek does instead |
| --- | --- |
| *sh* | nothing — σ is always *s*. **σιωπή** is *siopí*, never *shiopí*. |
| *ch* as in *church* | nothing in the standard language — τσ is *ts* |
| *j* as in *jam* | τζ is close but it is *dz* |
| the English *r* | ρ is a tap |
| the schwa — the *a* in *about* | nothing. Every Greek vowel is fully pronounced, always. |
| *w* | nothing. **ου** before a vowel is the nearest thing. |
| long and short vowel pairs | nothing. Five vowels, one length. |

**The schwa is the biggest single thing to unlearn.** English reduces unstressed vowels to a mumble: *banana* has three different *a* sounds. Greek does not reduce at all — **θάλασσα** has three identical *a* sounds, and giving the unstressed ones an English mumble is immediately audible.

**Which means: full vowels, every syllable, with the stress carried by loudness and length rather than by the other vowels collapsing.** That one correction does more for a Greek accent than anything else on this page.

**What Greek does with foreign sounds it lacks.** It substitutes: *sh* becomes σ, *ch* becomes τσ, *j* becomes τζ, *w* becomes ου or β. Hence **σαμπουάν** (shampoo), **τσεκ** (cheque), **Τζον** (John), **ουίσκι** (whisky).

**Practice.** Hold a hand in front of your mouth and say **πόλη, τώρα, κάνω** with no puff of air, ten times. Then say **θάλασσα** with three equal *a* sounds, ten times. Then **ώρα, τρία, ρολόι** with one tap each. Then say **σιωπή** and make sure the σ never becomes *sh*.
Punctuation, and the question mark that:
Small, and it will stop you misreading sentences from the first day of stage 2.

| Mark | Greek name | What it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **.** | τελεία | full stop, as in English |
| **,** | κόμμα | comma, as in English |
| **;** | ερωτηματικό | **the question mark** |
| **·** | άνω τελεία | the semicolon — a raised dot |
| **!** | θαυμαστικό | exclamation mark |
| **…** | αποσιωπητικά | ellipsis |
| **«  »** | εισαγωγικά | quotation marks |
| **'** | απόστροφος | apostrophe, for elision |
| **-** | ενωτικό | hyphen |

**The two to actually remember:**

1. **; is a question mark.** **Τι κάνεις;** means *how are you?* — it is not a clause joined to something.
2. **· is the semicolon.** A raised dot, mid-height. Rare in ordinary modern writing; common in older and church texts.

**Quotation marks are angled** — «Γεια σου» — though curly English-style quotes are increasingly common online. Dialogue in books often uses a dash instead:

— Καλημέρα.
— Καλημέρα, τι κάνεις;

**The apostrophe marks elision**, which is extremely common in speech and writing both: a final vowel drops before a word beginning with a vowel.

- **σε αγαπώ** → **σ' αγαπώ** (I love you)
- **από εδώ** → **απ' εδώ** (from here)
- **να το** → **να 'το** (there it is)

**Which means you will meet words you cannot find in a dictionary** because a letter is missing. The apostrophe is the clue; put the vowel back and look again.

**No capitals after a colon** and generally lighter capitalisation than English, as the capitals lesson said.

**Numbers use the European convention**: a comma for the decimal point and a full stop or space for thousands. **1.500,50** is one thousand five hundred and fifty cents. This matters for prices and will matter in a shop.

**Dates are day/month/year** — **14/10/2026** — and the month is often written out: **14 Οκτωβρίου 2026**, in the genitive.

**Practice.** Read these aloud and say whether each is a question: **Τι κάνεις; · Καλά, ευχαριστώ. · Πού είσαι; · Είμαι εδώ.** Then write **σ' αγαπώ** and **απ' εδώ** by hand, then write out what each is short for.
Numbers 0 to 20:
The first real vocabulary, and one grammatical surprise inside it.

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | μηδέν | 11 | έντεκα |
| 1 | ένα | 12 | δώδεκα |
| 2 | δύο | 13 | δεκατρία |
| 3 | τρία | 14 | δεκατέσσερα |
| 4 | τέσσερα | 15 | δεκαπέντε |
| 5 | πέντε | 16 | δεκαέξι |
| 6 | έξι | 17 | δεκαεφτά |
| 7 | εφτά | 18 | δεκαοχτώ |
| 8 | οχτώ | 19 | δεκαεννιά |
| 9 | εννιά | 20 | είκοσι |
| 10 | δέκα | | |

**The teens are simply δέκα plus the digit**, written as one word: δεκατρία, δεκατέσσερα, δεκαπέντε. No irregularities at all, which is kinder than English.

**Two spellings for four of them.** εφτά / επτά, οχτώ / οκτώ, εννιά / εννέα, δεκαεφτά / δεκαεπτά. The first of each pair is the everyday spoken form; the second is the older, more formal one, and it is what you will see in writing, on documents and in church. Both are correct and you will hear both.

**The surprise: three of these inflect.** Greek numbers are mostly fixed, but **1, 3 and 4 change with the gender** of what they count:

| | masculine | feminine | neuter |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | ένας | μία | ένα |
| **3** | τρεις | τρεις | τρία |
| **4** | τέσσερις | τέσσερις | τέσσερα |

- **ένας άντρας** (one man) · **μία γυναίκα** (one woman) · **ένα παιδί** (one child)
- **τρεις άντρες** · **τρεις γυναίκες** · **τρία παιδιά**

**Why this is in the alphabet stage.** Because gender is coming in stage 2 and it is better to have met it once, in the simplest possible place, than to meet it first as a rule. Also because you need numbers immediately — prices, times, the collection plate, how many of something you want.

**ένα is also the word for "a"** — **ένα παιδί** is both *one child* and *a child*. Greek has an indefinite article and it is the number one, as in Spanish and Italian.

**Counting aloud is the standard first fluency drill.** Count to twenty, out loud, every day this week; then count down from twenty, which is harder and better.

**Practice.** Count 0 to 20 aloud, three times. Then count back from 20. Then say: **ένας άντρας, μία γυναίκα, ένα παιδί, τρία παιδιά, τέσσερις γυναίκες**. Then write 1 to 10 in Greek words, by hand, with their accents.
Greek letters as numbers:
A small system you will meet in exactly the places you care about: church books, chapter numbers, school years and dates on monuments.

**Each letter has a numeric value.** The first nine letters are the units, the next nine the tens, the next nine the hundreds:

| | | | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Α΄ | 1 | Ι΄ | 10 | Ρ΄ | 100 |
| Β΄ | 2 | Κ΄ | 20 | Σ΄ | 200 |
| Γ΄ | 3 | Λ΄ | 30 | Τ΄ | 300 |
| Δ΄ | 4 | Μ΄ | 40 | Υ΄ | 400 |
| Ε΄ | 5 | Ν΄ | 50 | Φ΄ | 500 |
| ΣΤ΄ | 6 | Ξ΄ | 60 | Χ΄ | 600 |
| Ζ΄ | 7 | Ο΄ | 70 | Ψ΄ | 700 |
| Η΄ | 8 | Π΄ | 80 | Ω΄ | 800 |
| Θ΄ | 9 | — | — | — | — |

**The mark after the letter** — ΄, called a *κεραία* — is what says "this is a number". Before the letter and below the line, it multiplies by a thousand: **͵Α** is 1000.

**Six is the odd one.** The ancient letter *stigma* (ϛ) held the place; modern Greek writes **ΣΤ΄** instead. So a school year **ΣΤ΄ Δημοτικού** is the sixth class of primary school.

**Composite numbers add up, largest first**: **ΙΑ΄** is 11, **ΚΕ΄** is 25, **ΡΝΒ΄** is 152.

**Where you will actually see this:**

- **Church books and lectionaries** — chapters, psalms, tones. The eight tones of Byzantine chant are Α΄ to Πλ. Δ΄.
- **Icon and monument inscriptions**, including dates.
- **School years** — Α΄ Γυμνασίου, Β΄ Λυκείου.
- **Numbered rulers and patriarchs** — Κωνσταντίνος ΙΑ΄.
- **Lists and outlines**, where English would use roman numerals.

**It is not used for ordinary numbers.** Prices, times, phone numbers, dates in a newspaper: all Arabic numerals, as in English.

**The connection to the later curriculum.** This is the numbering system of the New Testament manuscripts, the service books and the Fathers, so learning it now is a small piece of that curriculum done early. It also explains **ΙΧΘΥΣ** and the other acrostics, and why **ΧΣ** on an icon is an abbreviation rather than a number.

**Practice.** Write 1 to 10 in Greek letters with their κεραία. Then read these: **Ε΄, ΙΒ΄, Κ΄, ΡΝΒ΄**. Then find a church book or an icon photograph and read one number off it.
Listening from day one:
You cannot understand anything yet and listening still starts today. This lesson is what to listen to, and what listening is for at this stage.

**What it is for now:** the sounds, the rhythm and the shape of words — not meaning. Your ear has to stop hearing Greek as a wash and start hearing it as syllables before any of the comprehension work can begin, and that takes weeks of exposure rather than study.

**The free material, in the order it becomes useful:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Pimsleur 1** | half an hour a day, answering out loud. It is the spoken foundation and it needs nothing you have not got. |
| **Language Transfer — Complete Greek** | 120 free audio lessons. Start it now and run it alongside Pimsleur; it explains the grammar by reasoning rather than drilling, and the first twenty lessons need no reading at all. |
| **Super Easy Greek** | the easiest tier of the Easy Greek videos, with Greek and English subtitles. Watch with subtitles, then without, then with again. |
| **The Easy Greek beginner podcast** | two voices, slowly, free |
| **Comprehensible-input channels** | Helinika, TPRS Beginners Greek, Comprehensible Greek, Slow Greek — all free, all designed to be understood before you can translate |
| **Greek music** | not study, and genuinely useful for the rhythm. stixoi.info has the lyrics of essentially everything. |
| **The FSI audio** | drills, one unit at a time, with the book. Dated, thorough, and his already. |

**How to listen, and this is the whole method at this stage:**

1. **Listen for the word boundaries.** Where does one word stop? That is the first thing a new ear cannot do.
2. **Listen for the stress** in each word, since Greek marks it and you now know it matters.
3. **Repeat out loud** — the single most valuable thing, and the reason listening and speaking are not separate habits.
4. **Do not translate.** At this stage understanding is a bonus and imitation is the point.

**Fifteen to thirty minutes a day**, and it counts as practice. Passive listening while doing something else is worth something but much less; attentive listening with repetition is worth a lot.

**The church is your best listening resource and the hardest one.** The social language before and after the service is exactly the Greek you are learning; the service itself is the older language. Listening to the former deliberately, every week, is a resource no app can match.

**Practice.** Do Pimsleur lesson 1 today, answering out loud. Then watch one Super Easy Greek video twice, with subtitles and then without. Then play any Greek song and try to mark the word boundaries in one line.
Reading from day one: signs, labels and:
You can already read every letter, which means you can read a great deal of real Greek without knowing any grammar. This lesson is how to use that.

**The easiest real Greek in the world is a shop sign**, because the words are nouns, they are isolated, and half of them are international:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **ΦΑΡΜΑΚΕΙΟ** | pharmacy |
| **ΑΡΤΟΠΟΙΕΙΟ** | bakery — *bread-making place* |
| **ΚΡΕΟΠΩΛΕΙΟ** | butcher — *meat-selling place* |
| **ΖΑΧΑΡΟΠΛΑΣΤΕΙΟ** | patisserie — *sugar-shaping place* |
| **ΤΡΑΠΕΖΑ** | bank |
| **ΕΞΟΔΟΣ** | exit |
| **ΕΙΣΟΔΟΣ** | entrance |
| **ΑΝΟΙΧΤΑ / ΚΛΕΙΣΤΑ** | open / closed |
| **ΩΘΗΣΑΤΕ / ΕΛΞΑΤΕ** | push / pull |
| **ΤΑΜΕΙΟ** | cash desk |
| **ΠΡΟΣΟΧΗ** | caution |

**The -ειο ending means "place where"**, which unlocks dozens of sign words at once: *αρτοποιείο, κρεοπωλείο, βιβλιοπωλείο* (bookshop), *ξενοδοχείο* (hotel — *stranger-receiving place*), *νοσοκομείο* (hospital), *ιατρείο* (surgery).

**Then labels.** A packet of something in a Greek shop, or in your own kitchen if anything is imported: **γάλα** (milk), **ψωμί** (bread), **ζάχαρη** (sugar), **αλάτι** (salt), **λάδι** (oil), **νερό** (water), **τυρί** (cheese), **ελιές** (olives).

**Then menus**, which are the most motivating reading there is: **σουβλάκι, γύρος, τζατζίκι, χωριάτικη** (village salad), **μουσακάς, παστίτσιο, σπανακόπιτα** (spinach pie), **φραπέ, ελληνικός καφές**.

**Then the church notice board**, which is the reading that matters most to you: the week's services, the feast, the names of the saints, the time. It is short, it repeats weekly, and it is the same vocabulary every time — which makes it the best graded reader available to you.

**And then graded reading proper**, from stage 2: the Greek school textbooks at ebooks.edu.gr, which are free, written for children learning to read their own language, and therefore exactly right. The first-year reading books are fully within reach by the end of stage 2.

**The rule, the same as everywhere in this curriculum:** read what you can read without stopping. Signs now, labels this week, menus and notices from stage 2.

**Practice.** Read the sign list aloud, with the stress worked out from the vocabulary you know. Then find five Greek words on packaging, a sign or a photograph and read them aloud. Then write down three words you saw and could not read, and look them up.
Review: the script and the sounds:
The end of stage 1. What should be true, and what stage 2 does.

**What should now be true:**

- You can read any Greek word aloud, correctly, including words you have never seen.
- All twenty-four letters, both cases, by name.
- The five vowel sounds, and the fact that *ι η υ ει οι* all say *i*.
- The vowel digraphs, and that **και** is *ke*.
- **αυ** and **ευ** as *af/av* and *ef/ev*, by what follows.
- **μπ ντ γκ γγ** as *b d g*, and **τσ τζ** as *ts dz*.
- **γ** soft before *a o u* and a *y* before *e i* — and **γεια σου** said right.
- **δ** and **θ** as the two English *th* sounds, **χ** as the *loch* sound, **ρ** as one tap.
- Double consonants written and not doubled in speech.
- The accent: compulsory, one per word, on one of the last three syllables, and the reason **πότε** and **ποτέ** are different words.
- The handwriting, lower case and capitals, and the ξ that still looks wrong.
- A Greek keyboard layout that works, with the accent key.
- **;** is a question mark and **·** is the semicolon.
- Numbers 0 to 20, with ένας/μία/ένα, τρεις/τρία, τέσσερις/τέσσερα.
- The alphabetic numerals, for church books and school years.
- Ten greetings and the first exchange, out loud, with the singular/plural politeness fork.
- Pimsleur and Language Transfer both started; Super Easy Greek in the week.

**What stage 1 deliberately did not do.** No grammar, no cases, no verbs beyond a handful of memorised phrases. Spelling was explained and not yet drilled — that starts now, as its own track.

**What stage 2 does.** First Greek: **είμαι** and **έχω**, the three genders, the article that changes with them, the noun in the nominative and the accusative, the present tense of the two verb classes, and enough sentence patterns to say what something is, where it is, what you want and what you have. It is the A1 level, and by the end of it you can hold a short conversation.

**And the two tracks open.** **Spelling 1** starts with stage 2 — the *i* spellings and the endings, which is where most of the leverage is. **Forms 1** starts with stage 3, when there are enough nouns and verbs for a table to be worth having.

**The honest check on stage 1.** The one thing people skip here is reading aloud, and it is the thing the whole stage was for. If you have been reading the examples silently, go back through three lessons and say everything out loud. It is the difference between a reader and a speaker, and the people at church will only ever meet the speaker.

**Practice.** Go down the list. Then read the first-exchange table aloud from memory. Then say **καλημέρα** to someone this Sunday.
The shape of a Greek sentence:
Before any grammar: what a Greek sentence looks like, and the one freedom it has that English does not.

**The default order is the English one.** Subject, verb, object:

- **Ο Γιώργος γράφει ένα γράμμα.** — George is writing a letter.
- **Το παιδί τρώει ψωμί.** — The child is eating bread.

**But the order can move, and moving it means something.** All of these are correct Greek and they differ in emphasis rather than in meaning:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Ο Γιώργος γράφει ένα γράμμα.** | neutral |
| **Γράφει ένα γράμμα ο Γιώργος.** | the writing is the news |
| **Ένα γράμμα γράφει ο Γιώργος.** | it is *a letter* he is writing, not something else |

**How that is possible.** Because Greek nouns change their form according to their job in the sentence — the subject looks different from the object — word order does not have to carry that information. English, with almost no case endings left, must keep *the dog bit the man* in that order or the meaning flips. Greek can say it in several orders and stay unambiguous.

**That system of endings is called case**, and it is the subject of the next several lessons and of all of stage 3. It is the central fact of Greek grammar.

**The subject can be left out entirely**, and usually is:

- **Γράφω ένα γράμμα.** — I am writing a letter. No word for *I*.
- **Είμαι εδώ.** — I am here.

**Why.** The verb ending already says who. **γράφω** can only mean *I write*; **γράφεις** can only mean *you write*. So **εγώ** (I) is added only for emphasis or contrast — *εγώ* γράφω, όχι αυτός. Using it in every sentence is one of the clearest marks of a foreign speaker.

**One more structural fact**: Greek has no verb *to do* for questions and no *-ing* form. **Γράφεις;** is both *do you write?* and *are you writing?*, and the question is marked by the voice rising and by the question mark **;** — nothing is reordered.

**So the first sentences you build need three things**, which are the next three lessons: the verb **είμαι**, the gender of nouns, and the article that goes with them.

**Practice.** Read aloud: **Ο Γιώργος γράφει ένα γράμμα. · Γράφω ένα γράμμα. · Είμαι εδώ. · Γράφεις;** Then say the first sentence three ways, moving the subject, and say out loud what each version emphasises.
είμαι — I am:
The first verb, and the one you will use most. It is irregular, it is short, and it is worth knowing cold today.

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **είμαι** | *íme* | I am |
| **είσαι** | *íse* | you are (one person, familiar) |
| **είναι** | *íne* | he / she / it is |
| **είμαστε** | *ímaste* | we are |
| **είστε** | *íste* | you are (plural or polite) |
| **είναι** | *íne* | they are |

**είναι does double duty** — *is* and *are*. Greek makes no distinction in the third person, so **είναι** covers he, she, it and they. Context tells you which.

**Sentences you can make immediately:**

- **Είμαι ο Γιώργος.** — I am George.
- **Είσαι καλά;** — Are you well?
- **Είναι εδώ.** — He is here. / She is here. / They are here.
- **Είμαστε Έλληνες.** — We are Greeks.
- **Δεν είμαι Έλληνας.** — I am not Greek.

**δεν** before the verb makes it negative, and it has its own lesson shortly.

**No word for *am* on its own**, and no helper verb: **είμαι καλά** is *I am well*, two words. There is also no *there is* — that is **υπάρχει**, a different verb, later in this stage.

**είναι does not mean "it is" in weather or time expressions the way English uses it.** **Κάνει ζέστη** is *it is hot* (literally *it makes heat*); **Είναι τρεις** is *it is three o'clock*. Both are later lessons; the point for now is that **είναι** is not an all-purpose *it is*.

**The polite form is the plural.** **Είστε καλά;** to someone older, someone you have just met, or the priest. **Είσαι καλά;** to a friend. This fork runs through every verb in Greek and it has a lesson of its own in this stage.

**Stress matters here**: **είμαι** is stressed on the first syllable, **είμαστε** on the first, **είστε** on the first. Nothing in this verb is stressed on the ending, which makes it easy.

**Practice.** Say all six forms aloud, five times, down the column. Then say these out loud: *I am here · you are well · we are Greeks · they are here · I am not George*. Then answer out loud: **Είσαι καλά;** — and **Είστε Έλληνας;**
The three genders:
Every Greek noun is masculine, feminine or neuter, and the gender is not negotiable. It decides the article, the adjective and the plural.

**Gender is grammatical, not biological.** **Ο καφές** (coffee) is masculine, **η καρέκλα** (chair) is feminine, **το βιβλίο** (book) is neuter, and none of that says anything about coffee, chairs or books.

**For people, grammar and sex usually agree**: **ο άντρας** (man), **η γυναίκα** (woman), **ο πατέρας** (father), **η μητέρα** (mother). The famous exception is **το παιδί** (child), which is neuter — and so is **το κορίτσι** (girl), by the same ending.

**You can usually tell the gender from the ending**, which is the practical news:

| Ending | Gender | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **-ος** | usually masculine | ο δάσκαλος, ο φίλος, ο δρόμος |
| **-ας, -ης** | masculine | ο πατέρας, ο άντρας, ο μαθητής |
| **-α, -η** | feminine | η γυναίκα, η μέρα, η πόλη, η αγάπη |
| **-ο, -ι** | neuter | το βιβλίο, το παιδί, το σπίτι |
| **-μα** | neuter | το μάθημα, το πρόβλημα, το όνομα |
| **-ος** | sometimes neuter | το δάσος, το μέγεθος — a small set, stage 3 |

**So the ending gives you the gender nine times out of ten**, and the exceptions are learnable: **η οδός** (street) and **η νήσος** (island) are feminine despite the -ος, and they are the kind of word that turns up on signs.

**Learn every noun with its article.** Not *δάσκαλος* but **ο δάσκαλος**; not *πόλη* but **η πόλη**. The article is part of the word as far as your memory is concerned, and every card in the deck carries it. This is the single most useful habit in the whole of Greek vocabulary learning, and skipping it costs years.

**Why gender matters so much.** Everything else agrees with it: the article (**ο, η, το**), the adjective (**καλός, καλή, καλό**), the pronoun, and the shape of the plural. Get the gender wrong and three other words come out wrong with it.

**Diminutives change gender freely**, which is worth knowing early because Greeks use them constantly: **ο καφές** → **το καφεδάκι**, **η γυναίκα** → **το γυναικάκι**, **το παιδί** → **το παιδάκι**. The **-άκι** ending is always neuter.

**Practice.** Say these ten nouns aloud with their articles, five times: **ο δάσκαλος, ο πατέρας, ο μαθητής, η γυναίκα, η μέρα, η πόλη, το βιβλίο, το παιδί, το σπίτι, το μάθημα**. Then guess the gender of these from their endings and check: **δρόμος, θάλασσα, κορίτσι, όνομα, άντρας, αγάπη**.
The definite article:
*The* in Greek is three words, and it changes again in the plural and in every case. It is the most frequent word in the language and the backbone of the whole grammar.

**In the nominative — the form for the subject of a sentence:**

| | Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Masculine** | ο | οι |
| **Feminine** | η | οι |
| **Neuter** | το | τα |

- **ο δάσκαλος** → **οι δάσκαλοι** · **η γυναίκα** → **οι γυναίκες** · **το παιδί** → **τα παιδιά**

**Note that οι is the plural for both masculine and feminine.** And note that **οι** is pronounced *i*, exactly like **η** — the spelling distinguishes them, the sound does not.

**Greek uses the article far more than English does.** It goes with:

- **Proper names, in speech.** **Ο Γιώργος** είναι εδώ — *George is here*. Leaving it out sounds formal or foreign.
- **Possessives.** **Ο φίλος μου** — *my friend*, literally *the friend of me*.
- **Abstract nouns.** **Η αγάπη** — *love*, as a thing in general.
- **Countries, usually.** **Η Ελλάδα**, **η Αγγλία**, **η Κύπρος**.
- **Languages, when the noun is meant.** **Τα ελληνικά** — *Greek*, the language.

**Where it is left out:** after **είμαι** with a profession or a nationality — **Είμαι δάσκαλος** (*I am a teacher*), **Είμαι Έλληνας** — and in most vocatives, when you call someone by name.

**The article tells you the gender, so it tells you a lot.** Hearing **η** before an unfamiliar word tells you it is feminine; hearing **τα** tells you it is a neuter plural. In fast speech the article often carries more grammatical information than the noun.

**It is also how you handle any noun you do not know.** If you need a word you have not learned, you still know it needs an article, and getting the article right is half of sounding correct.

**The accusative forms are next**, and the genitive is stage 3. Those three cases plus the vocative are the whole system.

**Practice.** Say these with the right article, out loud: *δρόμος, θάλασσα, παιδί, όνομα, πατέρας, πόλη, βιβλίο, γυναίκα*. Then put each into the plural with its plural article. Then read aloud: **Ο Γιώργος και η Μαρία είναι εδώ. · Τα παιδιά είναι καλά. · Η αγάπη είναι μεγάλη.**
ένας, μία, ένα — a and an:
The indefinite article, which is also the number one, and which has one awkward form worth getting right early.

| | Nominative | Accusative |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Masculine** | ένας | έναν |
| **Feminine** | μία / μια | μία / μια |
| **Neuter** | ένα | ένα |

- **ένας δάσκαλος** — a teacher · **μία γυναίκα** — a woman · **ένα παιδί** — a child

**It is the number one, exactly as in Spanish and Italian.** **Ένα παιδί** is both *one child* and *a child*, and context decides. If you need to insist on the number, **ένα μόνο παιδί** — *only one child*.

**μία and μια are the same word.** Written **μία** it is two syllables and usually means *one*; written **μια** it is one syllable and usually means *a*. Both spellings are correct and both are common; in speech it is almost always the quick one-syllable *mia*.

**The accusative masculine is έναν**, with the **-ν**: **Θέλω έναν καφέ** — *I want a coffee*. This is the first place the final **-ν** shows up and it is genuinely heard in speech, because it assimilates to the next sound: *énaŋ gafé*.

**There is no plural.** English *some books* is simply **βιβλία** — the noun on its own:

- **Θέλω ένα βιβλίο.** — I want a book.
- **Θέλω βιβλία.** — I want some books.

**Greek leaves the indefinite article out more than English does**, especially after **είμαι**:

- **Είμαι δάσκαλος.** — I am a teacher. Never *είμαι ένας δάσκαλος*.
- **Έχω αυτοκίνητο.** — I have a car. The article is optional, and leaving it out is the more natural reading: *I have a car* as a fact about me rather than one particular car.

**Which is a useful distinction to hear.** **Έχω ένα αυτοκίνητο** counts cars. **Έχω αυτοκίνητο** says you are a person who drives.
