| **όμορφος** | good-looking | **ξανθός** | blond |
| **μελαχρινός** | dark-haired | **καστανός** | brown-haired |
| **γκρίζος / ασπρομάλλης** | grey-haired | **φαλακρός** | bald |
| **με γυαλιά** | with glasses | **με μούσι** | with a beard |

**Character:**

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **καλός** | good, kind | **ευγενικός** | polite, kind |
| **έξυπνος** | clever | **αστείος** | funny |
| **σοβαρός** | serious | **ήσυχος** | quiet |
| **ζωηρός** | lively | **εργατικός** | hard-working |
| **γενναιόδωρος** | generous | **υπομονετικός** | patient |
| **αυστηρός** | strict | **ντροπαλός** | shy |

**The sentence patterns:**

- **Είναι ψηλός και αδύνατος.** — He is tall and thin.
- **Έχει μαύρα μαλλιά και γαλανά μάτια.** — He has black hair and blue eyes.
- **Είναι πολύ καλός άνθρωπος.** — He is a very good person.
- **Μοιάζει με τον πατέρα του.** — He looks like his father.
- **Είναι σαν τον αδελφό μου.** — He is like my brother.

**The colours**, since hair and eyes need them:

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **μαύρος** | black | **άσπρος / λευκός** | white |
| **κόκκινος** | red | **μπλε** | blue (invariable) |
| **γαλανός / γαλάζιος** | light blue | **πράσινος** | green |
| **κίτρινος** | yellow | **καφέ** | brown (invariable) |
| **γκρι / γκρίζος** | grey | **ροζ** | pink (invariable) |

**The loanword colours do not inflect**: **μπλε, καφέ, ροζ, γκρι, μωβ** stay the same in every gender and case. The Greek ones agree normally.

**Age and family, from earlier lessons**, fold in here:

- **Είναι τριάντα χρονών, παντρεμένος, με δύο παιδιά.** — He is thirty, married, with two children.
- **παντρεμένος / παντρεμένη** — married · **ανύπαντρος** — unmarried · **χήρα** — widow

**And the social descriptions that place a person**, which is the Greek way:

- **Είναι ο γιος του παπά.** — He is the priest's son.
- **Είναι από την Κύπρο.** — He is from Cyprus.
- **Είναι ο νονός του παιδιού μου.** — He is my child's godfather.

**Practice.** Describe five people you know out loud, in three sentences each: what they look like, what they are like, and who they are to you. Then describe yourself. Then write one of the descriptions down, checking every adjective's agreement.
Describing a place:
The other production lesson, and the vocabulary that lets you talk about where you live and where you are from — which is the second question anyone asks.

**Places:**

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **η πόλη** | city, town | **το χωριό** | village |
| **η χώρα** | country | **η γειτονιά** | neighbourhood |
| **ο δρόμος** | street, road | **η πλατεία** | square |
| **το κέντρο** | the centre | **τα προάστια** | the suburbs |
| **η θάλασσα** | sea | **το βουνό** | mountain |
| **το νησί** | island | **ο ποταμός** | river |
| **το λιμάνι** | harbour | **η παραλία** | beach |

**Buildings and what you need:**

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **το σπίτι** | house | **η πολυκατοικία** | block of flats |
| **το διαμέρισμα** | flat | **ο κήπος** | garden |
| **το μαγαζί** | shop | **η αγορά** | market |
| **το σχολείο** | school | **το νοσοκομείο** | hospital |
| **η τράπεζα** | bank | **το φαρμακείο** | pharmacy |
| **το εστιατόριο** | restaurant | **η ταβέρνα** | taverna |
| **το καφενείο** | the old-style café | **η καφετέρια** | the modern one |

**Describing it:**

- **Μένω σε μια μικρή πόλη στην Αγγλία.** — I live in a small town in England.
- **Είναι κοντά στη θάλασσα.** — It is near the sea.
- **Έχει πολλά μαγαζιά και δύο εκκλησίες.** — It has a lot of shops and two churches.
- **Είναι ήσυχα.** — It is quiet. (impersonal, neuter)
- **Μου αρέσει πολύ.** — I like it a lot.

**The adjectives for places**: **μεγάλος, μικρός, ήσυχος** (quiet), **θορυβώδης** (noisy), **όμορφος** (beautiful), **παλιός** (old), **μοντέρνος** (modern), **ακριβός** (expensive), **καθαρός** (clean), **βρόμικος** (dirty), **πολύβουος** (busy).

**Where you are from, in full:**

- **Είμαι από την Αγγλία, από μια πόλη που λέγεται York.** — I am from England, from a town called York.
- **Γεννήθηκα στη Νότια Αφρική.** — I was born in South Africa. (a past tense, stage 6 — use it as a phrase)
- **Μένω εδώ δέκα χρόνια.** — I have lived here ten years.

**Countries and nationalities**, with the pattern:

| Country | Man | Woman | Language |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| η Ελλάδα | Έλληνας | Ελληνίδα | ελληνικά |
| η Αγγλία | Άγγλος | Αγγλίδα | αγγλικά |
| η Κύπρος | Κύπριος | Κύπρια | — |
| η Νότια Αφρική | Νοτιοαφρικανός | Νοτιοαφρικανή | — |
| η Γερμανία | Γερμανός | Γερμανίδα | γερμανικά |
| η Ρωσία | Ρώσος | Ρωσίδα | ρωσικά |

**The nationality noun is capitalised, the language is not**: **Είμαι Άγγλος** but **μιλάω αγγλικά**.

**Practice.** Describe where you live in five sentences, out loud. Then describe Greece, or Cyprus, in three. Then answer **Από πού είσαι;** in full — country, town, how long you have been where you are.
The case system, in one place:
The whole noun system, now complete: four cases, three genders, two numbers. One page to come back to.

**The article, which is the frame everything hangs on:**

| | Masc. sg. | Fem. sg. | Neut. sg. | Masc. pl. | Fem. pl. | Neut. pl. |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Nominative** | ο | η | το | οι | οι | τα |
| **Accusative** | τον | την | το | τους | τις | τα |
| **Genitive** | του | της | του | των | των | των |

**The nouns, one example of each pattern, all four cases:**

| | ο δάσκαλος | ο πατέρας | ο μαθητής | η γυναίκα | η πόλη | το βιβλίο | το παιδί | το μάθημα |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Nom. sg.** | δάσκαλος | πατέρας | μαθητής | γυναίκα | πόλη | βιβλίο | παιδί | μάθημα |
| **Acc. sg.** | δάσκαλο | πατέρα | μαθητή | γυναίκα | πόλη | βιβλίο | παιδί | μάθημα |
| **Gen. sg.** | δασκάλου | πατέρα | μαθητή | γυναίκας | πόλης | βιβλίου | παιδιού | μαθήματος |
| **Voc. sg.** | δάσκαλε | πατέρα | μαθητή | γυναίκα | πόλη | βιβλίο | παιδί | μάθημα |
| **Nom. pl.** | δάσκαλοι | πατέρες | μαθητές | γυναίκες | πόλεις | βιβλία | παιδιά | μαθήματα |
| **Acc. pl.** | δασκάλους | πατέρες | μαθητές | γυναίκες | πόλεις | βιβλία | παιδιά | μαθήματα |
| **Gen. pl.** | δασκάλων | πατέρων | μαθητών | γυναικών | πόλεων | βιβλίων | παιδιών | μαθημάτων |

**What each case does, in one line each:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Nominative** | the subject — and the complement of είμαι |
| **Accusative** | the object, everything after a preposition, and time phrases like *την Κυριακή* |
| **Genitive** | *of*, possession, the indirect object with pronouns, dates, age |
| **Vocative** | addressing someone, with no article |

**The four observations worth carrying:**

1. **The article carries the case more reliably than the noun does.** In most of this table, the noun's ending is shared between two or three cells and the article distinguishes them.
2. **Neuters distinguish nothing** except the genitive.
3. **Feminines distinguish only the genitive** in the singular.
4. **The genitive is where every gender changes**, which is why it needed its own stage.

**The stress rules that go with it**, all three from the same source — the rule of limitation:

- **-ος** masculines move the stress forward in the genitive and accusative plural if it was on the third syllable from the end.
- **-ι** neuters put the stress on the genitive ending: **παιδιού, παιδιών**.
- **-ση** feminines move it in the plural: **πόλεων, κυβερνήσεων**.

**What is left for the Forms track**, which opens now: all of this as reference tables, with the less common patterns, the irregulars, and the adjectives and pronouns in full. Use it as a place to look things up rather than a thing to read once.

**Practice.** Rebuild the article table from memory, out loud. Then take any five nouns from the deck and give all eight forms of each. Then find three sentences in your reading where the article is the only thing telling you the case.
Talking about your family and your paris:
The production lesson for stage 3: everything from the last thirty lessons, used to talk about the people around you — which is what this curriculum is for.

**The genitive is the engine of it**, because Greek places people by whose they are.

**Family, in sentences:**

- **Είμαι ο [name], ο άντρας της [name].** — I am X, the husband of Y.
- **Έχω δύο παιδιά, ένα αγόρι και ένα κορίτσι.** — I have two children, a boy and a girl.
- **Ο γιος μου είναι δέκα χρονών.** — My son is ten.
- **Η κόρη μου πάει στο σχολείο.** — My daughter goes to school.
- **Ο πατέρας μου είναι από τη Νότια Αφρική.** — My father is from South Africa.
- **Η οικογένεια της γυναίκας μου μένει εδώ.** — My wife's family lives here.

**The parish:**

- **Πάω στην εκκλησία κάθε Κυριακή.** — I go to church every Sunday.
- **Ο πατέρας Γιώργος είναι ο ιερέας μας.** — Father George is our priest.
- **Η Λειτουργία είναι στις δέκα.** — The Liturgy is at ten.
- **Μαθαίνω ελληνικά για την εκκλησία και για τους φίλους μου.** — I am learning Greek for the church and for my friends.
- **Δεν καταλαβαίνω τη Λειτουργία, αλλά μαθαίνω.** — I do not understand the Liturgy, but I am learning.

**That last sentence is worth memorising exactly**, because it is both true and the one that will get you the most help. Greeks are, as a rule, delighted by a foreigner learning the language and will slow down for you the moment you say something like it.

**The questions you will be asked**, and they come in this order roughly every time:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Από πού είσαι;** | Where are you from? |
| **Πόσο καιρό μαθαίνεις ελληνικά;** | How long have you been learning Greek? |
| **Γιατί μαθαίνεις ελληνικά;** | Why are you learning Greek? |
| **Έχεις πάει στην Ελλάδα;** | Have you been to Greece? |
| **Είσαι Ορθόδοξος;** | Are you Orthodox? |
| **Έχεις παιδιά;** | Do you have children? |
| **Τι δουλειά κάνεις;** | What work do you do? |

**Prepare an answer to each**, out loud, in two or three sentences. That is a five-minute job and it is the difference between a conversation and a polite nod. The questions do not vary much, so a prepared answer is not a cheat — it is what fluency in a first conversation actually consists of.

**And the thing to say when you lose the thread**, from stage 2 and worth repeating:

- **Συγγνώμη, δεν κατάλαβα.** — Sorry, I did not understand.
- **Μπορείτε να το πείτε πιο αργά;** — Could you say it more slowly?
- **Πώς το λένε στα ελληνικά;** — How do you say it in Greek?

**Practice.** Write and then say aloud a two-minute self-introduction: who you are, where you are from, your family, why you are learning Greek, and your parish. Then answer the seven questions above out loud, twice each.
Reading: moving up a level:
What to read at the end of stage 3, and how to tell when to move up.

**The target now: Γλώσσα Β΄ Δημοτικού** — the second year of primary school, free at ebooks.edu.gr. Longer sentences than the first year, past tenses throughout, and real stories rather than captioned pictures.

**Also now within reach:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Ανθολόγιο Α΄–Β΄ Δημοτικού** | the reader: folk tales, poems, rhymes |
| **Children's books**, any | Greek editions of what you already know are ideal |
| **The church notice board**, in full | now including the feasts and the names |
| **Simple news headlines** | the headline only, not the article |
| **Song lyrics**, with the song playing | stixoi.info |
| **Instagram and Facebook posts** from Greek friends and parishes | short, modern, idiomatic |

**The test for whether a text is at your level**, and it is the same test as for sight-reading in a music curriculum: can you read a page aloud, understand the gist, and stop no more than once or twice. If you stop five times a page, go easier. If you stop never, go harder.

**How to move up without stalling:**

1. **Reread what you have read.** The second pass of a page you half-understood is worth more than a new page.
2. **Read aloud**, still — it is the speaking practice you cannot otherwise get.
3. **Look up only what blocks the sentence.** Two or three words a page.
4. **Keep a list of the words you looked up**, and card the ones that come up twice.
5. **Expect past tenses you have not met.** Stage 6 explains them; for now, recognise the shape and read on.

**Extensive against intensive reading.** Both are useful and they are different exercises: **extensive** is a lot of easy text for fluency, **intensive** is a short hard text taken apart completely. Do mostly extensive at this stage, with one intensive passage a week — a paragraph of a story, analysed down to every ending.

**Where the Forms track and the reading meet.** When you hit a form you cannot parse — a genitive plural, an unfamiliar declension — that is what the Forms tables are for. Looking it up takes thirty seconds and makes the next occurrence free.

**One genuinely motivating target**: by the end of stage 5 you will be able to read a short children's book start to finish. That is six months of this habit and it is the moment Greek stops being a subject and starts being a language you read.

**Practice.** Download **Γλώσσα Β΄ Δημοτικού**. Read its first story aloud, twice. List the words that blocked you and card the ones you would want again. Then read one page of **Γλώσσα Α΄** and notice how much easier it has become.
Listening: when to move up:
The listening habit at the end of stage 3 — what to use now, and the honest test for whether it is working.

**What you should have been doing since stage 1**: Pimsleur daily, Language Transfer alongside, and some Super Easy Greek. If any of that has lapsed, this is the lesson to restart it in.

**What is new at this level:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Easy Greek, the main tier** | not just Super Easy — real speed, dual subtitles |
| **The Easy Greek beginner podcast** | two speakers, slowly, free, and transcripts available |
| **Helinika's comprehensible-input series** | stories at a measured pace |
| **Greek children's cartoons** | dubbed Peppa Pig is a serious resource and nobody admits it |
| **Greek music with the lyrics open** | and now you can follow the grammar in them |
| **The parish hall** | the real one. Listen deliberately for ten minutes without trying to join in. |

**The test for level**, parallel to the reading one: can you follow the gist of a clip at normal speed with subtitles, and about half of it without. If subtitles give you nothing, it is too hard. If you need no subtitles at all, it is too easy.

**The three stages of listening to one clip**, and doing all three is the method:

1. **Without subtitles**, once. Get what you can.
2. **With Greek subtitles**, once or twice. Notice the words you heard wrongly — not the ones you did not know, the ones you misheard. That gap is the real listening problem.
3. **Without subtitles again.** It will be dramatically clearer, and that clarity is the thing being trained.

**What to listen *for* at this stage**, specifically:

- **The articles.** They carry the case and they are tiny and fast. Hearing **του** against **τον** is a real skill.
- **The final -ς**, which distinguishes *you* from *he* in every verb.
- **The weak pronouns** clustering before the verb — **μου το**, **της τα** — which sound like one word.
- **The stressed syllable**, which is your anchor for recognising a word you know.

**Why the parish is your best and worst resource.** Best, because it is the exact Greek you want, spoken by the people you want to talk to, free, weekly. Worst, because it is fast, overlapping, dialectal in places, and full of family references you cannot follow. Treat ten minutes of it as a listening exercise rather than a failure.

**A realistic expectation for the end of stage 3**: you catch names, greetings, numbers, the topic of a conversation, and complete short sentences addressed directly to you. You do not follow a conversation between two Greeks at speed. That comes around stage 6 to 8, and it comes suddenly.

**Practice.** Take one Easy Greek clip and do the three-stage method on it. Then at church this week, stand in the hall for ten minutes and count how many words you catch — not sentences, words. Write the number down and do it again in a month.
Writing with cases:
The writing habit, raised to the level of the grammar you now have: five sentences a day, each one containing a case you have to think about.

**The new requirement: every sentence must contain a genitive.** That is the forcing function, because the genitive is the case you will otherwise avoid.

**Examples at the right level:**

- **Το σπίτι του πατέρα μου είναι μεγάλο.**
- **Η γυναίκα του δασκάλου είναι από την Κύπρο.**
- **Τα παιδιά των γειτόνων παίζουν στον δρόμο.**
- **Το όνομα της κόρης μου είναι Μαρία.**
- **Η Λειτουργία της Κυριακής είναι στις δέκα.**

**Then the self-check, which is the actual exercise.** For each sentence, ask:

1. **Is every noun's gender right?** Check the article.
2. **Is every case right?** Subject nominative, object accusative, after a preposition accusative, possessor genitive.
3. **Does every adjective agree** in gender, number and case?
4. **Is the accent on every word of two syllables or more?**
5. **Is each *i* and *o* the right one?** Verbs **-ω**, nouns **-ο**; **-ει** a verb, **-η** a feminine noun.

**Five questions, five sentences, ten minutes.** The checking is where the learning is — writing without checking just records your current errors.

**Where to verify**: the Triantafyllidis dictionary at greek-language.gr for any noun's inflection, Lexiscope for any form at all, and the Forms track's tables for the patterns.

**Add one harder sentence a week**: a genitive plural, which is the form you will avoid hardest. **Τα παιδιά των φίλων μου**, **η γλώσσα των Ελλήνων**, **οι γονείς των μαθητών**.

**Write by hand at least some of it**, for stage 1's reason: the hand makes you decide the letter shapes and the spelling in a way typing does not.

**What to write about**, so that the habit survives: the day, the week, the parish, your family, what you are going to do. Real content in simple grammar beats invented content in complicated grammar.

**And keep them.** The notebook from stage 2 now has a month or two in it. Read the first page and the last page back to back — that comparison is the clearest measure of progress you will get, and it is worth doing every month or so.

**Practice.** Write five sentences now, each with a genitive. Then run the five-question check on each. Then write one sentence with a genitive plural and verify it against the dictionary.
Review: stage 3:
The end of stage 3, which completes the noun system. What should be true, and what stage 4 does.

**What should now be true:**

- The full article table — eighteen cells, nine words — automatic.
- The genitive: what it is for, and its seven jobs.
- The genitive of all three genders, singular and plural, with the stress shifts.
- The genitive plural in **-ων**, including **-εων**, without flinching.
- Possession both ways, and the chains: **το όνομα της γυναίκας του αδελφού μου**.
- Names in the genitive and the vocative, including saints' days.
- Dates, age and duration.
- The indirect object: genitive pronouns, **σε** plus a noun, and never a genitive noun.
- The vocative, with no article, and **Πάτερ**.
- **κύριε, κυρία**, and **κυρία Μαρία** as the register English does not have.
- Adjectives in all four cases, the **-ος/-α/-ο** variant, **πολύς**, **όλος**, **λίγος**.
- Comparatives with **πιο** and with **-τερος**, superlatives, and the five irregulars.
- All the pronouns, strong and weak, and which goes where.
- **που** for every relative clause, **ο οποίος** after a preposition, **ό,τι** against **ότι**.
- The indefinites, with **δεν** where they need it.
- Numbers in the genitive — **τριών, τεσσάρων** — and the ordinals.
- The neuter **-ος** nouns and the common irregulars.
- What moving a word in a sentence does, and the doubled pronoun that comes with it.
- Quantities and measures, with no preposition between them and the thing.
- The weather and the impersonal verbs, including **πρέπει να**.
- You can describe a person and a place, and talk about your family and your parish.
- Reading **Γλώσσα Β΄ Δημοτικού**; listening with the three-pass method; five written sentences a day with a genitive in each.

**What stage 3 deliberately did not do.** Still no past tense, no future, and no aspect. Everything has been in the present — which is why you can describe but not yet narrate.

**What stage 4 does, and it is the hinge of the whole curriculum.** Aspect: the fact that nearly every Greek verb has two stems, one for actions seen as ongoing and one for actions seen as complete, and that the choice between them is compulsory in the past, the future and the subjunctive. With it come **να**, the subjunctive, the imperative, and the whole verb system opening up.

**It is the hardest thing in the language for an English speaker** and it is where the time in this curriculum is concentrated. Everything before it has been preparation; everything after it depends on it.

**And the Forms track opens now**, with the noun, adjective and pronoun tables you have just learned as permanent reference. Start **Forms 1** this week.

**Practice.** Go down the list. Then say your two-minute self-introduction again, and notice how much more of it has genitives in it than it did a month ago.
What the Forms track is for:
**Forms track, module 1 of 5. Run this module alongside stage 3**, at about one of these lessons for every three or four route lessons, alternating with the Spelling track.

**What it is.** The declension and conjugation tables, in full, as reference. Not an explanation — the route lessons explain — but the complete paradigms in one place, so that when you meet a form you cannot parse you have somewhere to look it up in thirty seconds.

**Why a track rather than appendices.** Three reasons:

1. **The tables are needed before they can be learned.** You will meet **των πόλεων** in your reading long before you could produce it, and a lookup is the right response.
2. **They are drill material.** A table is something to recite, cover and rebuild — the same six-step drill as the Spelling track, applied to forms instead of letters.
3. **They are a reading tool.** Parsing an unfamiliar form backwards — *which pattern has a genitive plural in -εων?* — is how you work out what a word is, and tables are what make it possible.

**How to use a module here, which is not how you use a route lesson:**

- **Read it once**, to know what is in it.
- **Come back to it** whenever a form stops you.
- **Drill one table a week**: recite it, cover it, rebuild it on paper, check.
- **Do not try to memorise all of it in order.** The forms stick through use and through the deck; the tables are for the gaps.

**What is in the five modules:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Forms 1** | the article, the pronouns, and every noun and adjective pattern — with stage 3 |
| **Forms 2** | the verb in the present and the imperfective: both classes, the mediopassive, the irregulars — with stage 4 |
| **Forms 3** | the perfective stems: how they are formed, the common irregular pairs, and the aorist — with stage 4 and 6 |
| **Forms 4** | the full tense table, the subjunctive, the imperative, the participles and the passive — with stage 6 and 7 |
| **Forms 5** | the numerals in full, the learned declensions that survive in formal Greek, and the irregular verbs as a reference list — with stage 9 |

**Where the authoritative versions are**, when this track is not enough: the **Triantafyllidis dictionary** at greek-language.gr gives every noun and verb its full inflection; **Lexiscope** inflects anything you type; and the **official school grammar** at ebooks.edu.gr is the standard reference, free, and written for native children — which makes it unusually clear.

**One habit worth adopting now.** When you look a form up, say the whole paradigm aloud rather than just the cell you needed. It costs ten seconds and it is how a table stops being a lookup and becomes knowledge.

**Practice.** Read the next lesson's article table and recite it aloud. Then cover it and write it out. Then do the same with one noun table of your choice.
The article and the pronouns, in full:
The reference page for the two most frequent word-classes in the language.

**Practice.** Recite the article table, then the two pronoun tables, down the columns. Then cover and rebuild all three on paper. Then find a sentence in your reading with three articles in it and name each one's case.
Masculine nouns: every pattern:
Every masculine declension pattern in the modern language, with its stress behaviour.

**-ος, stressed on the third syllable from the end** — the stress moves:

| | Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Nom.** | ο άνθρωπος | οι άνθρωποι |
| **Acc.** | τον άνθρωπο | τους ανθρώπους |
| **Gen.** | του ανθρώπου | των ανθρώπων |
| **Voc.** | άνθρωπε | άνθρωποι |

**-ος, stressed on the last or second-last** — nothing moves:

| | Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Nom.** | ο φίλος · ο ουρανός | οι φίλοι · οι ουρανοί |
| **Acc.** | τον φίλο · τον ουρανό | τους φίλους · τους ουρανούς |
| **Gen.** | του φίλου · του ουρανού | των φίλων · των ουρανών |

**-ας:**

| | Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Nom.** | ο πατέρας | οι πατέρες |
| **Acc.** | τον πατέρα | τους πατέρες |
| **Gen.** | του πατέρα | των πατέρων |
| **Voc.** | πατέρα | πατέρες |

**-ης:**

| | Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Nom.** | ο μαθητής | οι μαθητές |
| **Acc.** | τον μαθητή | τους μαθητές |
| **Gen.** | του μαθητή | των μαθητών |

**-ης with -δες plural** — a sizeable spoken group:

| | Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Nom.** | ο μανάβης | οι μανάβηδες |
| **Gen.** | του μανάβη | των μανάβηδων |

**-ες and -ους** — small, common, and irregular:

| | Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Nom.** | ο καφές · ο παππούς | οι καφέδες · οι παππούδες |
| **Acc.** | τον καφέ · τον παππού | τους καφέδες · τους παππούδες |
| **Gen.** | του καφέ · του παππού | των καφέδων · των παππούδων |

**-έας** — formal, and the priest is in it:

| | Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Nom.** | ο ιερέας | οι ιερείς |
| **Acc.** | τον ιερέα | τους ιερείς |
| **Gen.** | του ιερέα | των ιερέων |

**The irregulars worth listing:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **ο γιος** | του γιου · οι γιοι · τους γιους |
| **ο άντρας** | του άντρα · οι άντρες |
| **ο μήνας** | του μήνα, formal **του μηνός** |
| **ο Χριστός** | του Χριστού · voc. **Χριστέ** |
| **ο Θεός** | του Θεού · voc. **Θεέ** — and the formula **Θεέ μου** |

**The two rules that cover the whole page:**

1. **The singular drops the -ς in the accusative**, and the vocative is **-ε** for **-ος** nouns and the bare stem for the others.
2. **The genitive plural is -ων**, always.

**Practice.** Recite **ο άνθρωπος** and **ο μαθητής** in all eight forms. Then cover the page and give all eight of **ο φίλος**, **ο πατέρας** and **ο καφές**. Then find a masculine noun in your reading whose pattern you cannot name, and place it here.

Every feminine pattern, including the three that behave unlike the rest.

**-α, with the stress anywhere:**

| | Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Nom.** | η γυναίκα · η θάλασσα | οι γυναίκες · οι θάλασσες |

| --- | --- | --- |

| **Acc.** | την αδελφή | τις αδελφές |
| **Gen.** | της αδελφής | των αδελφών |

| | Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Nom.** | η πόλη · η τάξη | οι πόλεις · οι τάξεις |
| **Acc.** | την πόλη | τις πόλεις |
| **Gen.** | της πόλης | **των πόλεων** |

**-ος** — feminine with masculine endings:

| | Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Nom.** | η οδός · η μέθοδος | οι οδοί · οι μέθοδοι |
| **Acc.** | την οδό | τις οδούς |

| | Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Nom.** | η αλεπού | οι αλεπούδες |
| **Gen.** | της αλεπούς | των αλεπούδων |

**The learned -ις / -εως**, which you will read and not say:

| | Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Nom.** | η πόλις (archaic) | αι πόλεις |
| **Gen.** | **της πόλεως** | των πόλεων |

**της πόλεως** turns up in formal names and signs — **Δήμος Αθηναίων**, **Τράπεζα της Ελλάδος** — and recognising it as the old genitive of **η Ελλάδα** is the point. **Της Ελλάδος** and **της Ελλάδας** are the same word in two registers.

**The irregulars:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **η μητέρα** | regular **-α**, voc. **μητέρα** |
| **η κόρη** | της κόρης · οι κόρες |
| **η γιαγιά** | της γιαγιάς · οι γιαγιάδες |
| **η Παναγία** | της Παναγίας — the feast is **της Παναγίας** |
| **η Κυριακή** | της Κυριακής — and it means both *Sunday* and the name |

**The two rules:**

1. **The singular changes only in the genitive**, which adds **-ς**.
2. **The genitive plural is -ων**, with **-εων** for the **-ση/-ξη/-ψη** nouns, and the stress on the ending.

**Practice.** Recite **η γυναίκα** and **η πόλη** in all six forms. Then cover and rebuild **η αδελφή**, **η τάξη** and **η οδός**. Then find a street sign's genitive and say which pattern it belongs to.

| | Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Nom.** | το γράψιμο | τα γραψίματα |
| **Gen.** | του γραψίματος | των γραψιμάτων |

**The irregulars:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **το γάλα** | του γάλακτος · no common plural |
| **το νερό** | του νερού · τα νερά — regular **-ο** |
| **το γεγονός** | του γεγονότος · τα γεγονότα |
| **το οινόπνευμα** | normal **-μα**, and the word on the bottle |
| **το Πάσχα** | indeclinable |
| **το ευρώ** | indeclinable |

**Indeclinable neuters are a real and growing group** — loanwords and some borrowings keep one form for everything: **το ευρώ, το ταξί, το μετρό, το σινεμά, το πάρτι, το σπορ, το τρένο** (which does inflect: του τρένου). When in doubt with a recent loanword, leaving it unchanged is usually right.

**The rules:**

1. **Three cases share one form**, in both numbers.
2. **The genitive singular is -ου, -ιού, -ματος, -ους or -τος**, by pattern.
3. **The genitive plural is -ων**, always, with the stress following the pattern.

**Practice.** Recite **το παιδί** and **το μάθημα** in all four forms. Then cover and rebuild **το βιβλίο**, **το δάσος** and **το φως**. Then list five indeclinable neuters you already use.

How to use a declension table:
The last lesson of this module, and the one that makes the rest of the track pay: how to go from a form you have met to the word it belongs to.

**The problem.** You are reading and you meet **των συνεντεύξεων**. You do not know the word, and the dictionary lists words in the nominative singular. You have to work backwards.

**The procedure:**

1. **Identify the case and number from the ending and any article.** **των** means genitive plural, immediately.
2. **Strip the ending.** **-εων** off **συνεντεύξεων** leaves **συνεντεύξ-**.
3. **Ask which pattern has that genitive plural.** **-εων** is the **-ση / -ξη / -ψη** feminines.
4. **Rebuild the nominative singular.** **συνεντεύξ-** plus **-η** gives **η συνέντευξη** — interview.
5. **Look it up and check.** The dictionary confirms it, and now the word is yours in all its forms.

**The diagnostic endings**, which is the table to actually use:

| You see | It is |
| --- | --- |
| **-ου** | genitive singular — masculine **-ος** or neuter **-ο** |
| **-ους** | accusative plural masculine, or genitive singular of a neuter **-ος** noun |
| **-ων** | genitive plural, any gender |
| **-εων** | genitive plural of a **-ση/-ξη/-ψη** feminine |
| **-ας** | genitive singular feminine **-α**, or nominative singular masculine |
| **-ης** | genitive singular feminine **-η**, or nominative singular masculine |
| **-εις** | nominative or accusative plural of a **-ση** feminine |
| **-ματος** | genitive singular of a **-μα** neuter |
| **-ιού** | genitive singular of an **-ι** neuter |
| **-ες** | nominative or accusative plural feminine, or masculine **-ας/-ης** |
| **-οι** | nominative plural masculine |
| **-α** | neuter plural, or feminine singular, or neuter **-μα** singular |

**The ambiguities are real and the article resolves most of them.** **-ας** could be two things; **της** or **ο** in front of it decides. This is why the article is the most useful word in the language for reading, as stage 2 claimed.

**When the stem itself has changed**, which happens in the irregulars: **του φωτός** → **το φως**, **του γάλακτος** → **το γάλα**, **των γυναικών** → **η γυναίκα**. Those are learned rather than derived, and they are the twenty or so words this module lists as irregular.

**The tools that do it for you**, and using them is not cheating: **Lexiscope** takes any form and tells you its lemma and its full paradigm; the **Triantafyllidis dictionary** accepts inflected forms in its search. Use them, and then say the paradigm aloud so that the lookup teaches you something.

**The habit to build.** Every time you look a form up, write the nominative singular and the genitive plural in your notebook. Two forms per word is enough to place it in a pattern forever, and the deck will carry the rest.

**Practice.** Work backwards from these five forms to their dictionary entries, using the diagnostic table: **των ανθρώπων · της κυβερνήσεως · τα μαθήματα · του παιδιού · τις πόλεις**. Then do the same with three forms from your current reading.
